slides.source: M4, Section 4.10, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M04_Conjoint_Segmentation_and_CLV.md

slides.title: Validation and Market Transfer
bullets: Hold out respondents or tasks according to the intended use.
Check coding, price units, and probabilities.
Relate stated preference to awareness, distribution, and availability.
slides.notes: A survey share is conditional on the experiment. Real demand also depends on who sees the offering and whether they can buy it. The demand forecast needs an explicit transfer assumption.
slides.source: M4, Section 4.4, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M04_Conjoint_Segmentation_and_CLV.md

slides.title: mHealth Product Economics
bullets: Food logs reveal recorded use and category histories.
A paid-plan choice model needs additional price and preference evidence.
Financial scenarios can state the missing inputs explicitly.
slides.notes: The lecture notes use an imposed paid-plan logit example separately from observed logs. Behavioral logging segments do not establish willingness to pay or paid subscription retention.
slides.source: M4, Section 4.11, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M04_Conjoint_Segmentation_and_CLV.md

slides.title: AI-Assisted Conjoint Analysis
bullets: Provide the choice-set identifier and the selected alternative.
Require probabilities to sum to one within each task.
Preserve respondent groups in validation.
Request a portfolio comparison with explicit margins.
slides.notes: A code generator may accidentally normalize probabilities over the full dataset or treat repeated tasks as independent respondents. Small constructed tasks expose those errors.
slides.source: M4, Section 4.10, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M04_Conjoint_Segmentation_and_CLV.md

slides.title: Synthetic Consumers in Concept Screening
bullets: A shortlist directs the budget for human product research.
Generated reactions can suggest benefits and objections.
A screening claim needs evidence on new concepts and the intended customers.
slides.notes: The concept-screening study compares 57 personal-care concepts with 9,300 U.S. human responses (Maier et al., 2025). Semantic similarity rating maps generated text to five-category distributions using anchors manually optimized on those same surveys. For GPT-4o with image stimuli and averaged anchors, the reported 90.2% correlation attainment divides the concept-level correlation by a split-half human benchmark. Individual-rating accuracy, purchase prediction, and attribute tradeoffs require their own comparisons and a suitable response model.
slides.source: (Maier et al., 2025, Table 1, Appendix A.3). https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.08338v3

slides.title: Distribution Fit and Product Selection
slides.caption: Six synthetic concepts, 100 invented ratings each. Overall category shares match, while the preferred concepts differ.
slides.description: The left panel shows common overall shares of 0, 0, 22.5, 30, and 47.5 percent in categories 1–5. The right panel preserves concept A–F identity: reference means fall from 4.5 to 4.0, pooled means equal 4.25, reversed means rise from 4.0 to 4.5, and compressed means fall from 4.30 to 4.20. The right vertical scale is 3.9–4.6.
slides.notes: Across the equally weighted synthetic concepts, every candidate matches the reference’s aggregate category distribution, yet the pooled pattern removes the differences needed for product selection. The reversed rule selects F and E instead of A and B, while the compressed pattern preserves order and shrinks rating differences. These constructions isolate distinct failures that an aggregate distribution check can miss.

slides.title: A Screening Rule Needs a Decision Metric
slides.caption: Imposed comparisons on the same six concepts. A high distribution score can accompany a poor shortlist.
slides.notes: KS similarity is one minus the maximum cumulative-probability difference, averaged equally across concepts. Pearson compares concept means. Spearman gives the same results in this construction. Constant pooled means leave correlation undefined and every concept tied. Compressed means have a mean absolute rating error of 0.12 despite preserving the top two. The three candidates were constructed using the synthetic reference to isolate these properties, so this is an analytical comparison rather than a prospective prediction test.

slides.title: New Concepts and Human Validation
bullets: Separate anchor development, configuration selection, and final concepts.
Freeze the complete measurement procedure before final human outcomes.
Sample rejected concepts to reveal missed opportunities.
slides.notes: The complete procedure includes prompts, model version, generation settings, embedding, anchors, aggregation, and shortlist rule. Final concepts and human outcomes remain outside those choices. Human tests confined to the selected concepts cannot reveal promising exclusions. Known sampling probabilities for rejected concepts support population comparisons with appropriate uncertainty. Observed purchases and stated intent remain separate outcomes.

slides.title: Feature and Price Comparisons
slides.caption: Invented means. Auxiliary bias includes an overall shift and a price effect.
slides.description: At low price, primary means rise from 3.1 to 3.9 and auxiliary means from 3.3 to 4.1 when the feature changes from standard to premium. With the feature standard, raising price reduces the primary mean from 3.1 to 2.1 and raises the auxiliary mean from 3.3 to 3.5. Both panels use the same rating scale; navy circles denote primary and orange squares auxiliary means.
slides.notes: Feature and price are each coded -1 and +1. The imposed primary coefficients are (3, 0.4, -0.5), and auxiliary bias adds 0.8 + 0.6 times price. Both sources preserve the 0.8-point feature contrast, while their price contrasts have opposite signs. No human or model responses were collected. The Gaussian model treats the response as a continuous rating score.

slides.title: Research Accuracy and Source Allocation
slides.intro: Source precision is response count divided by known noise variance:
slides.interpretation: Primary precision $t$ identifies intercept and price. Both sources inform the feature through $t+s$.
slides.notes: Here t = N_P / sigma_P squared and s = N_A / sigma_A squared. The loss sums squared errors across the three primary coefficients with the fixed -1/+1 coding. Auxiliary bias is restricted to intercept and price. Known bias features, linear means, and independent Gaussian errors support the calculation. Full derivation and Python are in M4 Section 4.24.

slides.title: The Cost of Informative Responses
slides.caption: The saving depends on source costs, noise, and which response features bias can imitate.
slides.description: In the invented four-profile design, the orange curve approaches 33.33 percent asymptotic savings as the information-cost ratio approaches zero and reaches zero at one third. The navy dashed line stays at zero when bias includes every response feature. The open zero-cost endpoint is a limit.
slides.notes: The information-cost ratio is auxiliary cost times auxiliary variance divided by primary cost times primary variance. The criterion is worst-case MSE for the full three-coefficient primary vector. The one-third limit is specific to this design and loss. It is not a general rule that cost savings equal the share of unconfounded coefficients.

slides.title: Accuracy and Research Cost
slides.caption: Imposed costs: 1 and 0.01 per response. Rounded allocations save 23.68% at the same 0.01 MSE target.
slides.notes: With both source variances set to one, the mixed allocation places 54 primary and 324 auxiliary observations at each profile. The asymptotic calculation saves 24.29 percent; rounding each source-profile count upward yields the feasible allocation in the table, which need not be the exact integer optimum. A complete budget also includes setup, human validation, and monitoring costs. Reproduce the allocation with allocate_responses.py in the Auxiliary_Data example.

slides.title: Customer Alternatives and AI Pricing
bullets: Customer value depends on the offered outcome and implementation effort.
Better tools can make internal analysis a stronger alternative.
Lower seller costs and lower willingness to pay can occur together.
slides.notes: Under a quasilinear comparison, the buyer price ceiling is delivered value minus buyer burden and outside-option utility. Use a common customer and horizon. Product design can reduce integration and verification effort, while competitive improvements raise the value of the alternative. The conditional numerical comparison appears in Session 14 and M8 §8.17.

slides.title: Information and the Pricing Objective
slides.intro: Two synthetic restaurants: expected demand intercept $\widehat a$, cost $c=2$, substitution $\delta=0.5$.
slides.interpretation: Independent owners maximize their own profits. Joint pricing maximizes their combined profit.
slides.notes: Demand has two equally likely states with intercepts 10 and 14, and a common signal identifies the state correctly with probability r. Each independent firm chooses its price in dollars per meal equivalent while treating its rival’s price as fixed. A joint profit objective instead includes the rival’s profit, changing the price-setting incentive even when preferences, costs, and information remain fixed. M4 derives the interior solutions and supplies the complete program and quantity-corner checks.

slides.title: Profits and Consumer Surplus
slides.caption: Synthetic market; dollars per market-day. Costs and preferences stay fixed.
slides.description: Four bars stack total firm profit and consumer surplus for independent and joint pricing at signal accuracies 0.5 and 1. Bar height equals total welfare in the specified two-restaurant economy.
slides.notes: Within independent pricing, perfect information raises profit from 29.63 to 30.81 and reduces consumer surplus from 32.30 to 30.81. Mean posted price stays 5.33, while quantity-weighted paid price rises to 5.47. At accuracy 0.5, joint pricing raises profit to 33.33 and reduces consumer surplus to 19.33. These are different changes in an original model. No observed Wendy's outcome or legal conclusion is estimated.

slides.title: Price Presentation and Customer Understanding
bullets: A base price and a mandatory fee determine the total paid.
A stated-choice task can reveal different responses to equivalent totals.
The feasible pricing design depends on the applicable rule and industry.
slides.notes: The FTC's fee rule addresses live-event tickets and short-term lodging. Its scope should remain explicit. A response difference to fee framing does not itself authorize a particular presentation.
slides.source: FTC Rule on Unfair or Deceptive Fees FAQ. https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/rule-unfair-or-deceptive-fees-frequently-asked-questions

slides.title: The Same Ranking Leaves Welfare Unresolved
slides.caption: Same purchases and ranking: USD 4.80 gain or USD 4.90 loss per customer.
slides.description: Left: cumulative alternative-minus-baseline purchase changes of +5, −5, −5, and 0 percentage points across four rank cutoffs. Right: gains under value systems (100,2,1,0) and (100,99,98,0).
slides.notes: Synthetic one-product purchases have baseline probabilities (.40,.30,.20,.10) and alternative probabilities (.45,.20,.20,.15). Values are dollars per purchased product. The best and worst values and strict ranking agree across scenarios. Other burdens and prices are common; incremental procedure cost is zero. Expected values change from 40.80 to 45.60 in the first scenario and from 89.30 to 84.40 in the second. Independent checks and complete Python are in M4 §4.29.

slides.title: Identify the Valuation Premise
bullets: More top-ranked purchases can coexist with more bottom-ranked purchases.
Cardinal value gaps determine the balance.
Check every cumulative rank cutoff.
Justify procedure costs and customer permission separately.
slides.notes: If every cumulative change is nonnegative, consumption value weakly rises for every ordered value system. The example has mixed signs. Precise purchase measurement does not determine the value gaps. The comparison changes a welfare premise, while the previous demand-completion example changes an unobserved demand curve. Both remain conditional model exercises. Choosing a practice adds reasons about authorization and burdens.

slides.title: Product-Design Discussion
bullets: How much of C's demand comes from existing products?
Which design change would identify the price tradeoff?
What evidence could change the launch recommendation?
slides.notes: The recommendation depends on substitution, incremental contribution, and costs. An appealing new-product share can coexist with little category expansion.
slides.source: M4, Section 4.3, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M04_Conjoint_Segmentation_and_CLV.md

practice: Calculate choice probabilities and compare human and synthetic sampling costs at a common accuracy target.
application: Use 20 minutes for synthetic concept screening and human validation, followed by 10 minutes for demand information, pricing objectives, and customer surplus.

title: Segmentation and Customer Lifetime Value
objectives: Define similarity using economically meaningful customer features.
Evaluate segment stability and future outcomes.
Calculate lifetime value with consistent timing and distinguish retention concepts.
Compare clustering cost and final-center consistency with a common evaluation population.

slides.title: A Retention-Support Decision
bullets: A service team can support only some customers.
High baseline value and responsiveness to support are separate quantities.
Segments should correspond to feasible service decisions.
slides.notes: A segment with high predicted value may have little incremental response to outreach. The support decision needs the change in future contribution caused by the action, net of its costs.
slides.source: M4, Section 4.9, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M04_Conjoint_Segmentation_and_CLV.md

slides.title: Customer Features at a Common Date
bullets: Recency is time since the last eligible event.
Frequency counts events in a fixed window.
Monetary value uses sales or contribution over that window.
slides.notes: Customers with unequal exposure histories can appear different because of observation time. The feature definition must specify eligibility and whether returns affect sales or transaction counts.
slides.source: M4, Section 4.5, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M04_Conjoint_Segmentation_and_CLV.md

slides.title: K-Means and Similarity
slides.intro: Choose $K$ centers for transformed customer features $z_i$.
slides.interpretation: Scaling the features changes the distance and can change the segments.
slides.notes: K-means minimizes within-cluster squared Euclidean distance. A standardized feature receives a different implicit weight from the raw variable. The transformation is a substantive choice.
slides.source: M4, Section 4.5, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M04_Conjoint_Segmentation_and_CLV.md

slides.title: Units Change the Nearest Customer
slides.caption: Synthetic customers have unchanged spending and frequency records.
slides.description: Changing spending from dollars to hundreds of dollars reverses which customer is nearest to A. Frequency then receives more relative weight.
slides.notes: Compare A=(100,1), B=(110,9), and C=(200,1), then change only the unit used to express spending. The resulting change in distance shows why a numerical representation embeds a weighting of customer attributes. The appropriate weighting depends on the service decision.
slides.source: M4, Section 4.5, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M04_Conjoint_Segmentation_and_CLV.md

slides.title: Evaluating a Segmentation
bullets: Inspect segment size, profile, and actionable differences.
Compare stability across seeds, samples, and periods.
Evaluate outcomes that did not mechanically define the clusters.
slides.notes: Within-cluster dispersion declines as K rises. A high-spending cluster will have high spending by construction when spending is an input. Later outcomes provide a more informative descriptive check.
slides.source: M4, Section 4.6, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M04_Conjoint_Segmentation_and_CLV.md

slides.title: Similarity of Positive Mechanisms
slides.intro: For each paper, collect the mechanisms coded as present in a set $A_i$.
slides.interpretation: Jaccard distance ignores shared absences. Average linkage compares these distances.
slides.notes: Compare 48 retrieved papers with potential dual use or a reported choice concern using twelve binary codes, including social cues, emotion, disclosure, defaults, and exit friction. A zero means that a mechanism was not coded from reviewed evidence, so papers with missing reviews are excluded from the comparison. This distinction keeps unreviewed papers from appearing similar merely because evidence has not yet been assessed. M4 §4.17 provides the complete program.

slides.title: Social Influence is the Largest Cluster
slides.caption: 48 retrieved potential-risk reviews. Four clusters selected from K=2 through K=8.
slides.description: Social influence contains 19 papers, emotion and identity 15, disclosure/framing/defaults eight, and attention/search/control six. The horizontal scale runs from zero to the full sample of 48.
slides.notes: The largest cluster contains 39.6% of the sample. Emotion/identity is the most common overlapping feature at 21 of 48, so feature and cluster rankings differ. Almost all papers in this analysis are coded for inferred dual use. Counts do not measure market prevalence or author intent.

slides.title: Reproduce the Mechanism Grouping
slides.intro: Run from the Consumer_Agency_Literature folder after installing its requirements.
slides.code:
import pandas as pd
from cluster import FEATURES, select_sample, partition
df = pd.read_csv("coded_papers.csv")
sample = select_sample(df, "downloaded_risk")
labels, distances = partition(sample[FEATURES].to_numpy(), 4)
assert len(sample) == 48
slides.check: The complete script compares K values, exports profiles, and refits sensitivity samples.
slides.notes: The short snippet reproduces the selected four-cluster partition. The full cluster.py program in M4 Section 4.17 selects K using silhouette scores and checks aggregate counts. Stable paper identifiers preserve traceability to original summaries.

slides.title: The Coding Changes the Conclusion
bullets: Median subsample agreement: adjusted Rand index 0.794.
Changing one feature per paper lowers median agreement to 0.250.
The broader abstract-based sample selects eight clusters.
slides.notes: Subsamples contain 80% of the primary papers and hold K=4 fixed across 200 repetitions. One-bit changes are an imposed sensitivity exercise, retaining a positive feature per paper. These are conditional stability results, not confidence intervals for population harm. The broader 84-paper risk sample is purposefully selected and chooses the upper K boundary.

slides.title: mHealth Segments Use Earlier Histories
slides.caption: Eligible users have at least 30 observed days before July 1.
slides.description: Earlier logging frequency and recorded breadth distinguish clusters. Later logging does not enter the clustering inputs.
slides.notes: The representation uses first-half logging fraction, mean category breadth, and mean calorie-share variety. K=3 is imposed for the comparison. The scaler and centers use only the earlier window.
slides.source: M4, Section 4.11, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M04_Conjoint_Segmentation_and_CLV.md

slides.title: Later Logging by Earlier Segment
slides.caption: mHealth denominators use 182 earlier and 184 later calendar days.
slides.notes: Later absence contributes zero observed days for eligible users. The figures describe persistence in recorded activity. They are not contractual retention rates or effects of a service intervention.
slides.source: M4, Section 4.11, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M04_Conjoint_Segmentation_and_CLV.md

slides.title: Lifetime Value and Payment Timing
slides.intro: Value future contribution conditional on remaining active.
slides.interpretation: The period for margin $m_t$, discounting $d$, and retention must agree.
slides.notes: The acquisition cost a occurs at time zero. This convention excludes immediate contribution. If a current-period contribution is included, it must be added explicitly.
slides.source: M4, Section 4.7, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M04_Conjoint_Segmentation_and_CLV.md

slides.title: A Stationary Subscription
slides.intro: Suppose monthly retention is $r$ and monthly contribution is $m$.
slides.notes: The formula assumes constant retention and conditional margin and an infinite horizon, with the first payment one month later. It follows from a convergent geometric series.
slides.source: M4, Section 4.7, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M04_Conjoint_Segmentation_and_CLV.md

slides.title: Retention Has Nonlinear Value
slides.caption: Synthetic stationary model. Monthly margin, discounting, and acquisition cost stay fixed.
slides.description: CLV rises increasingly rapidly with retention. Increasing monthly retention from 0.80 to 0.90 raises value from about 178.57 to 440.91 dollars.
slides.notes: The high-retention region places more weight on distant contributions. Uncertainty about the persistence of retention and margins can dominate the valuation.
slides.source: M4, Section 4.7, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M04_Conjoint_Segmentation_and_CLV.md

slides.title: A Finite-Sum Check
slides.intro: Compare the closed form with 2,000 future monthly payments.
slides.code:
m, r, d, a = 60, 0.8, 0.01, 50
closed = m * r / (1 + d - r) - a
finite = sum(m * r**t / (1+d)**t
             for t in range(1, 2001)) - a
assert abs(closed - finite) < 1e-8
slides.check: Both calculations give approximately 178.57 dollars.
slides.notes: Matching the two expressions checks the payment convention and arithmetic. It does not establish constant retention as a valid model of a real relationship.
slides.source: M4, Section 4.7, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M04_Conjoint_Segmentation_and_CLV.md

slides.title: Cancellation and a Logging Gap
bullets: A subscription may record cancellation directly.
A 30-day logging gap is an operational activity event.
Observation can end before a defined event occurs.
slides.notes: Right censoring preserves the distinction between no observed event by the end of follow-up and an event at the last observation. A logging gap is not proof of permanent departure or paid cancellation.
slides.source: M4, Section 4.13, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M04_Conjoint_Segmentation_and_CLV.md

slides.title: The Event Definition Changes Survival
slides.caption: mHealth time-to-gap analysis uses a stated gap definition and observation horizon.
slides.description: Survival tracks time until a defined logging gap. The risk set and right censoring determine which histories contribute at each time.
slides.notes: Changing the gap length changes the event being measured. Survival of recorded activity should remain separate from contractual renewal in financial calculations.
slides.source: M4, Section 4.13, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M04_Conjoint_Segmentation_and_CLV.md

slides.title: Endpoint and Continuous Retention
bullets: Endpoint retention allows customers to leave and return.
Continuous retention requires uninterrupted presence.
Acquisition can include first entry, return, or switching.
slides.notes: A starting-provider cohort is fixed at the initial period. The same-provider, other-provider-only, and no-paid-provider states distinguish platform retention from category participation. Multiple providers require explicit overlap handling.
slides.source: M4, Section 4.14, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M04_Conjoint_Segmentation_and_CLV.md

slides.title: Coding Exercise: Segments and Value
bullets: Fit feature scaling and segments on an earlier period.
Describe a later period without refitting the groups.
Vary assumed paid retention in a separate CLV calculation.
slides.notes: The small CLV calculation is session_examples.py in the Lecture Examples folder S06. The real mHealth m04.py example and GenAI cohort program keep behavioral measurements separate from imposed financial inputs.
slides.source: M4, Section 4.11, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M04_Conjoint_Segmentation_and_CLV.md

slides.title: Cluster Mass Changes the Update
slides.intro: Earlier count 10, mean 2; current count 2, mean 7. Weight each batch by one-half.
slides.interpretation: Weighting the two means equally would give 4.5. e-means carries sums and counts.
slides.notes: In the synthetic scalar example, weighted mass determines how much each batch contributes to the updated cluster center. The complete e-means algorithm adds a cooling schedule and rules for unused clusters, so this calculation isolates one part of its operation. Batch order in shuffled static data also differs from calendar recency. Choosing a useful customer intervention requires a link from the resulting groups to customer outcomes beyond the fixed squared-distance objective.

slides.title: Final Centers Can Change Customer Labels
slides.caption: Recompute assignments before forming segment profiles.
slides.description: Four fixed scalar points are 0, 4, 5, and 10. Final centers 2 and 7.5 imply a boundary at 4.75. Point 5 changes from a blue circle in group A to an orange square in group B. With one of four labels changed, mean squared distance falls from 5.8125 to 5.125.
slides.notes: Saved labels can reflect earlier center locations. The constructed comparison holds all points and final centers fixed. Faiss e-means returns training-pass labels; a new assignment is necessary for a profile consistent with final centers. The exact fractions and denominator are reproduced by centroid_checks.py.

slides.title: Lower Error Has a Computational Cost
slides.caption: Common data, initial centers, and final scorer; method-specific budget caps.
slides.description: Median fitting milliseconds on the horizontal axis and held-out mean squared distance on the vertical axis compare Lloyd, MiniBatch, and CPU e-means. Points summarize three seeds for caps 2, 5, and 10. e-means attains lower error and takes longer than Lloyd at each corresponding cap. Shared final evaluation time is reported separately in the notes.
slides.notes: The reference run uses 50,000 training and 10,000 test vectors, 32 coordinates, 64 centers, one numerical thread, and training-only scaling. Caps denote different iterations or epochs and do not imply equal arithmetic work. Scikit-learn 1.6.1 and Faiss 1.16.0 supply the implementations. Times are short, machine-specific measurements. This is an original synthetic CPU comparison; no published GPU speedup is reproduced.

slides.title: From Numerical Groups to Marketing Actions
bullets: Check final labels, feature scale, and stability across initializations.
Compare the time needed for fitting and final assignments.
Justify the action using later outcomes, causal evidence, and customer choice.
slides.notes: At cap 2, the median e-means saved-label discrepancy is 9.408% of 50,000 valid training labels. The common evaluation costs more than fitting in the recorded runs. mHealth uses three earlier-window features and three centers, with later logging for descriptive interpretation. Faster fitting or smaller dispersion does not establish an effect of support. Jaccard mechanism clustering and affiliation communities use different objectives. o-means is optional large-K GPU reading and was not run.

slides.title: Retention and Effective Cancellation
bullets: High paid retention can reflect satisfaction or difficulty leaving.
Measure cancellation completion and unwanted subsequent charges.
Evaluate customer value alongside the seller's lifetime-value objective.
slides.notes: A customer who prefers cancellation can remain subscribed because of friction. The consumer-value comparison requires independent evidence about that preference and the available procedure.
slides.source: M8, Section 8.14, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M08_Current_Topics_and_Integrated_Decisions.md

slides.title: Geographic Usage Groups
slides.caption: Raw and standardized distances produce different geographic groups.
slides.description: Illinois groups contain 94, 347, and 812 areas. The adjusted Rand index comparing raw and standardized clustering is 0.805.
slides.notes: The three groups are a fixed descriptive example. Thirty random starts and four tested seeds yield the same standardized partition. Raw distances give more influence to the index with larger spread. Group names order mean MCI and carry no ranking of customer ability or value.

slides.title: Stable Groups Still Need Outcome Validation
bullets: Raw versus standardized partitions: adjusted Rand index 0.805.
Tested seed changes leave the standardized partition unchanged.
Observe requested assistance and task completion before allocating service.
slides.notes: Adjusted Rand agreement compares co-membership and is not a percentage of identical labels. Seed stability checks a computation under chosen features. Scaling changes the meaning of similarity. The public data contain no individual assistance need or service outcome, so no cluster is validated as a customer capability category.

slides.title: Retention Discussion
bullets: What action differs across the proposed segments?
Does a customer's absence represent churn or censoring?
Which retention assumption changes the support decision?
slides.notes: A useful recommendation identifies the response to intervention as well as baseline value. Cluster membership alone does not establish the effectiveness of differentiated support.
slides.source: M4, Section 4.9, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M04_Conjoint_Segmentation_and_CLV.md

title: Text, Social Media, and Networks
objectives: Define a text construct and evaluate labels on the deployment population.
Distinguish prevalence, text exposure, retrieval, and substantive interpretation.
Explain network reach and brokerage without inferring influence from correlation.
Distinguish citation presence from support using a controlled source comparison.
Trace how anchors, similarities, and persona weighting determine a text-based rating.
Compare feature preservation, group weighting, and access at original network origins.
Distinguish recorded-category agreement from the compatibility of a replacement text representation.
Use contextual coding, negative cases, and source comparison to assess utility cost-recovery claims.

slides.title: A Customer-Service Decision
bullets: A retailer wants to detect delivery complaints quickly.
The document may be a review, sentence, or service conversation.
The action is a review queue with limited staff capacity.
slides.notes: The unit and label definition determine the evaluation. A negative review can concern price, quality, or delivery. A classifier needs a construct that identifies the service action the manager can take.
slides.source: M5, Section 5.1, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M05_Text_Social_and_Network_Analysis.md

slides.title: Text Preparation
bullets: Keep negation and domain-specific terms when they affect meaning.
Document language, duplicates, and boilerplate.
Fit the vocabulary on training documents.
slides.notes: Removing the word not can reverse a sentiment label. Duplicate descriptions across train and test can produce a favorable score for a task requiring generalization to new text.
slides.source: M5, Section 5.2, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M05_Text_Social_and_Network_Analysis.md

slides.title: TF-IDF Representation
slides.intro: Weight a term by frequency in a document and rarity across documents.
slides.interpretation: Tokenization, smoothing, and normalization are implementation choices that need a record.
slides.notes: Different packages use different conventions. A rare word can be predictive without being substantively important. The vocabulary and IDF values must be learned from the training corpus.
slides.source: M5, Section 5.2, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M05_Text_Social_and_Network_Analysis.md

slides.title: Embeddings and Similarity
bullets: Embeddings place text in a numerical representation.
Nearby descriptions may share meaning or usage.
A useful similarity measure still requires domain validation.
slides.notes: A semantic model can confuse closely related foods that have distinct nutritional properties. A cosine score is a representation-based similarity, not a probability of label correctness.
slides.source: M5, Section 5.3, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M05_Text_Social_and_Network_Analysis.md

slides.title: A Text-to-Rating Measurement Rule
slides.intro: For one response and one anchor set, subtract the least similar category and normalize.
slides.interpretation: The similarities $s_r$ depend on the anchors and embedding. Equal similarities leave the denominator at zero.
slides.notes: This is the paper setting with epsilon zero and SSR temperature one. The normalized weights describe a mapping to rating categories. Calibration against human outcomes requires separate evidence. The course code explicitly abstains when the spread is at most 1e-12. That numerical threshold is not evidence of consumer indifference.
slides.source: (Maier et al., 2025, Table 1, Appendix A.3). https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.08338v3 M4 §4.23, M5 §5.23, and M7 §7.36. ../03_Data_and_Code/Synthetic_Consumers/README.md

slides.title: The Same Response Under Different Anchors
slides.caption: Fixed authored response and imposed similarities. The mean rating changes from 4.25 to 3.70.
slides.description: Paired bars show category weights 0, 5, 15, 30, and 50 percent for Set 1 and 0, 10, 30, 40, and 20 percent for Set 2. The probability assigned to categories 4 and 5 falls from 80 to 60 percent.
slides.notes: The response is: I would consider it if the refill is convenient and the total price is acceptable. The two sets express increasing purchase intent with different wording. The similarities are deliberately imposed, so their difference does not estimate the effect of these words on an embedding model. Across the supplied three concepts and two personas, Set 1 favors refillable body wash while Set 2 favors fragrance-free. Averaging sets does not establish validity against consumers.

slides.title: A Hand-Checkable Rating
slides.intro: Run from the Synthetic_Consumers example folder with the complete local program.
slides.code:
from anchor_measurement import rating_distribution

scores = [0.20, 0.23, 0.29, 0.38, 0.50]
weights = rating_distribution(scores)
value = sum((r + 1) * p for r, p in enumerate(weights))
assert abs(value - 4.25) < 1e-12
slides.check: Imposed inputs. The full program preserves persona weights and incomplete mappings.
slides.notes: Subtracting 0.20 yields 0, 0.03, 0.09, 0.18, and 0.30, whose sum is 0.60. The category weights are 0, 0.05, 0.15, 0.30, and 0.50. Average repeats within persona before averaging personas. For the refill example, equal-persona weighting gives 3.975 while counting an identical repeated response as another person gives 4.067. No model account is needed for this calculation.

slides.title: Labels, Sentiment, and Topics
bullets: Sentiment measures an evaluative construct.
Aspect labels distinguish the object of a complaint.
Topics summarize recurring term patterns under a model.
slides.notes: A high-weight topic term does not establish a causal driver of satisfaction. Topic names are interpretations that should be checked against representative documents.
slides.source: M5, Section 5.4, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M05_Text_Social_and_Network_Analysis.md

slides.title: Rare Complaints Lower Precision
slides.caption: Synthetic classifier. Sensitivity is 80% and specificity is 90%.
slides.description: At 1% prevalence, only about 7.5% of flagged reviews are true complaints. At 20% prevalence, precision rises to 66.7%.
slides.notes: The classifier has unchanged conditional error rates. The changing base rate alters the composition of the flagged group and therefore the workload of human reviewers.
slides.source: M5, Section 5.5, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M05_Text_Social_and_Network_Analysis.md

slides.title: Precision Depends on Prevalence
slides.intro: Let $\pi$ be complaint prevalence, $s$ sensitivity, and $c$ specificity.
slides.interpretation: False positives can dominate a queue when the target condition is rare.
slides.notes: The formula applies to the specified population and classifier. Use prevalence from the intended deployment population; an artificially balanced training set changes that share.
slides.source: M5, Section 5.5, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M05_Text_Social_and_Network_Analysis.md

slides.title: Expected Queue Composition
slides.intro: In 10,000 synthetic reviews, complaint prevalence is 1%.
slides.code:
n, prevalence = 10000, 0.01
sensitivity, specificity = 0.8, 0.9
tp = n * prevalence * sensitivity
fp = n * (1-prevalence) * (1-specificity)
precision = tp / (tp + fp)
assert round(precision, 4) == 0.0748
slides.check: The expected queue contains 80 true complaints and 990 false positives.
slides.notes: These are expected counts under the imposed rates. Actual counts vary. Capacity planning should consider the queue size as well as sensitivity.
slides.source: M5, Section 5.5, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M05_Text_Social_and_Network_Analysis.md

slides.title: Human and LLM Annotation
bullets: Write a label definition with difficult boundary examples.
Measure agreement and adjudicate disagreements.
Assess a held-out sample with human labels.
Record the model, prompt, and response format.
slides.notes: Agreement measures consistency, not necessarily construct validity. When a model labels the data used to evaluate itself, the resulting score can reproduce its own labeling choices. A sponsor-framing comparison can hold the same proposal fixed while varying whether the sponsor likes it. Evaluate factual criticism separately from approval. This is a proposed exercise motivated by Sharma et al.; no course model responses have been collected.
slides.source: M5, Section 5.6, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M05_Text_Social_and_Network_Analysis.md (Sharma et al., 2024), https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.13548v4. M5 §5.18.

slides.title: Agency Labels Need Supporting Evidence
bullets: Extract the outcome, mechanism, study design, and supporting passage.
Separate reported choice concerns from inferred possible misuse.
Retain uncertain cases and compare independent coding.
slides.notes: Consumer agency concerns understanding, choice, action, and revision or exit. Persuasion alone does not establish impairment. The current literature codes are preliminary AI-assisted annotations without independent human adjudication. Immersive Service supplies qualitative agency evidence; Nudging App Adoption supplies evidence about choice presentation whose misuse requires an additional inference. See M5 Section 5.16.

slides.title: mHealth Food Descriptions
bullets: Descriptions can recur across many users and dates.
A repeated-description split evaluates familiar language.
A held-out-description split tests generalization to new language.
slides.notes: The source category is an imperfect label. The same normalized description can have multiple source labels. Retaining that ambiguity lets the evaluation distinguish inconsistent labeling from classifier mistakes.
slides.source: M5, Section 5.10, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M05_Text_Social_and_Network_Analysis.md

slides.title: Familiar and New Text Are Different Tests
slides.caption: mHealth text classification uses the stated training and evaluation splits.
slides.description: The comparison separates repeated descriptions from new descriptions and identifies source-label ambiguity. Performance depends on the deployment question.
slides.notes: A random event split can place an identical description in both training and test. That may be useful for repeated lookup but overstate performance on new descriptions.
slides.source: M5, Section 5.10, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M05_Text_Social_and_Network_Analysis.md

slides.title: A New Encoder Changes the Coordinates
bullets: Compare word and character features on unseen descriptions.
Fit vocabulary, weights, directions, and alignment using training data.
Choose dimensions on validation; retain every test category.
Recorded categories define the target, including ambiguous labels.
slides.notes: The mHealth comparison gives equal weight to 6,000 training descriptions, 1,500 validation descriptions, and 1,500 test descriptions. Normalized descriptions are disjoint across splits, although users and periods are shared, so the test concerns new descriptions within that setting. Seventy-four test descriptions have multiple recorded categories; the modal category with alphabetical tie breaking defines the reference. Retaining categories such as default and recipe makes agreement with the recorded system the measured outcome. Nutritional correctness requires a separately justified reference.

slides.title: Topic Shares Need a Denominator
slides.caption: mHealth topic summaries compare documents, entries, and users under defined weights.
slides.description: A topic common in repeated entries can look less prevalent when distinct descriptions or equally weighted users form the denominator.
slides.notes: Long documents and repeated records can dominate term-weighted summaries. A business question about the fraction of affected customers needs a customer denominator.
slides.source: M5, Section 5.12, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M05_Text_Social_and_Network_Analysis.md

slides.title: Which Pricing Statements Deserve Review?
bullets: A retailer reviews competitors' public pricing communication.
A keyword occurrence supplies a reading lead.
Define the priced object, timing, and evidence before interpreting adoption.
slides.notes: The supplied corpus includes core terms for pricing methods and shelf-label infrastructure. Among observed calls, core-call rates are 2.90% in retail, 2.02% in restaurants, and 10.49% in the selected comparison group. These are call-weighted disclosure rates.
slides.source: M5, Section 5.14, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M05_Text_Social_and_Network_Analysis.md

slides.title: Speaking Time Changes the Comparison
slides.caption: Observed calls; heuristic roles. Management includes prepared remarks and Q&A.
slides.description: Management has 127 core occurrences in 16,685,338 words, versus analysts' 23 in 2,761,999 words. Rates are 0.076 and 0.083 per 10,000 words.
slides.notes: Raw counts rank management higher, whereas exposure-adjusted intensity is slightly higher for analysts. This is a descriptive arithmetic comparison, with different formats and heuristic labels. Restricting both counts and words to detected-Q&A calls gives rates of 0.072 and 0.083.
slides.source: M5, Section 5.14, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M05_Text_Social_and_Network_Analysis.md

slides.title: Same Vocabulary, Different Evidence
bullets: Amazon: current price information; Eventbrite: advertising cost per click.
Wendy's: planned tests; Kroger: shelf-label infrastructure.
A claim about use still requires evidence on implementation and outcomes.
slides.notes: Seven purposeful, source-linked paraphrases are provided in interpretation_cases.csv. They are examples of construct distinctions, not a representative precision sample. Delta's January 2025 question recorded as management/prepared also motivates reviewing heuristic speaker boundaries.
slides.source: M5, Section 5.14, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M05_Text_Social_and_Network_Analysis.md

slides.title: Match Counts and Words to the Same Calls
slides.intro: From the Earnings_Calls folder, compare the verified metadata.
slides.code:
from assessment import load_checked
from disclosure import role_rates
calls, mentions, _, _ = load_checked()
rates = role_rates(calls, mentions, require_qa=True)
assert rates.calls.eq(2240).all()
print(rates[['role', 'core_matches', 'per_10000_words']])
slides.check: Excluding a call removes both its occurrences and its words.
slides.notes: Run disclosure.py for group, quarterly, and role tables. The counterexample test includes one excluded call with many words; dropping only its matches would change the rate incorrectly.
slides.source: M5, Section 5.14, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M05_Text_Social_and_Network_Analysis.md

slides.title: Evaluate Retrieval and Interpretation Separately
bullets: A denial and a future intention can match the same phrase.
Relevant paraphrases can escape the dictionary.
Validate held-out firms or later calls with independently labeled hits and misses.
slides.notes: Run construct_checks.py for eight synthetic sentences. A purposeful case set cannot estimate corpus precision or recall. Probability sampling and appropriate weights are needed for population metrics. No external model or labeling API was run for the supplied course example.
slides.source: M5, Section 5.14, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M05_Text_Social_and_Network_Analysis.md

slides.title: What Does a Utility Disclosure Establish?
bullets: Identify the speaker, customer class, charge component, and horizon.
Separate a forecast, request, approval, and household outcome.
Compare recovery claims with offsetting revenues and protections.
slides.notes: The source set has six purposeful documents, including three calls, and ten claim records. Public coding uses original paraphrases and locators; the notes retain three short verbatim excerpts. Five documents were downloaded. The accounting passage was checked separately through a web reader. Counts describe this selection and provide no prevalence estimate. Hsieh and Shannon (2005), https://doi.org/10.1177/1049732305276687; O'Brien et al. (2014), https://doi.org/10.1097/ACM.0000000000000388; Gale et al. (2013), https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2288-13-117; O'Connor and Joffe (2020), https://doi.org/10.1177/1609406919899220; Braun and Clarke (2021), https://doi.org/10.1080/14780887.2020.1769238.

slides.title: Follow the Cost into the Bill
slides.caption: Each transition requires evidence appropriate to its institutional stage.
slides.description: Investment plans lead to recovery requests, then authorized charges and household bills. New-load revenue and protections can reduce the requested amount. Dashed arrows identify transitions requiring additional records.
slides.notes: A smaller requested increase can coexist with a higher bill than today. Electricity supply procurement differs from construction recovery. Check the legal entity and customer class before connecting passages across documents. A statement at one stage does not establish all subsequent outcomes.

slides.title: Keep the Case That Challenges Your Interpretation
bullets: Evergy discusses investment-related rate pressure and benefits from growing sales.
Its later request proposes a higher residential bill while claiming a revenue offset.
A lower bill than otherwise can still be a higher bill than today.
slides.notes: The later announcement proposes a USD 17.25 monthly increase at 1005 kWh, conditional on approval, and a USD 61 million reduction in the annual revenue request from anticipated data-center revenue. The comparison does not identify a data-center-specific causal effect. Read both sides of the account before developing an explanatory theme.

slides.title: Qualitative Quality Depends on the Analytical Approach
bullets: State selection rules, prior expectations, and changes to the codebook.
Compare within cases; retain source locators and negative cases.
Use independent review for the shared coding frame and explain disagreements.
slides.notes: This is directed content analysis with a codebook. Independent human coding has not yet been completed. Agreement would concern coding consistency, not the truth of a corporate statement. Reflexive thematic analysis makes different methodological commitments. Retain investigator interpretation and the limits of investor-facing documents. Hsieh and Shannon (2005), https://doi.org/10.1177/1049732305276687; O'Brien et al. (2014), https://doi.org/10.1097/ACM.0000000000000388; Gale et al. (2013), https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2288-13-117; O'Connor and Joffe (2020), https://doi.org/10.1177/1609406919899220; Braun and Clarke (2021), https://doi.org/10.1080/14780887.2020.1769238.
slides.source: M5 §5.27. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M05_Text_Social_and_Network_Analysis.md (Hsieh and Shannon, 2005), https://doi.org/10.1177/1049732305276687; (O'Brien et al., 2014), https://doi.org/10.1097/ACM.0000000000000388; (Gale et al., 2013), https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2288-13-117; (O'Connor and Joffe, 2020), https://doi.org/10.1177/1609406919899220; (Braun and Clarke, 2021), https://doi.org/10.1080/14780887.2020.1769238.

slides.title: Prompt Revision Uses Evaluation Evidence
bullets: A passage used to revise a prompt becomes development material.
Keep passages from one call together when constructing a split.
Freeze the prompt and reference-label procedure before fresh evaluation.
slides.notes: A test on new firms addresses a different deployment population from a test on later calls from familiar firms. Repeated passages are not independent firm-level replications. Evaluate a competent dictionary baseline with the same eligible evidence. Once final labels guide a revision, a later confirmation needs new evidence or a justified adaptive-evaluation design.

slides.title: Citations and Supporting Evidence
slides.caption: Four fictional pricing questions; authored answers and reference annotations.
slides.description: All four answers cite a source in every condition. Supported counts are four with curated sources, two after a misleading memo is added, and four after review. The contrast is stipulated.
slides.notes: The synthetic records support different kinds of statements: S1 reports a price increase and a before-after unit change without a causal design, S2 contains an unanswered question about discounts, and S3 defines a selected panel-member denominator. S4 incorrectly converts these records into claims of causality and a discount announcement. The comparison shows why citations must support the particular inference being made. Because no model responses were collected, the counts describe these constructed claims and establish no effect of context on model performance.

slides.title: A Controlled Source Comparison
bullets: Hold the questions, model version, and scoring rule fixed.
Use fresh conversations and preserve raw responses.
Repeat paired runs; randomize condition order.
Assess support independently and retain missing answers.
slides.notes: Run source_selection.py to reproduce the constructed example. In an optional live extension, supply the excerpts and questions without the saved answers or support labels. A single pair gives a descriptive comparison. Repetition helps separate sampling variation from a stable context effect. Credible contradictory evidence requires review; disagreement alone is not a reason to exclude a source. The class activity fits the existing earnings-call Python block.

slides.title: Generator and Judge Changes
slides.caption: Identical saved outputs are scored by both judges. All scores are stipulated.
slides.description: Old-judge scores are 60 and 62; new-judge scores are 75 and 77. The generator gain is two points within either judge, while the diagonal comparison is seventeen.
slides.notes: A stable judge supplies a common comparison but still requires validation. Position, verbosity, and self-preference can affect evaluation. For earnings-call summaries, independently check factual support, speaker role, and whether a statement concerns a plan or an implemented action. Preserve inconsistent judgments.
slides.source: M5 §5.18. (Zheng et al., 2023), https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05685; (Panickssery et al., 2024), https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.13076

slides.title: Network Objects
bullets: Nodes identify customers or accounts.
Edges represent a defined relationship in a time window.
Degree counts links, while brokerage concerns paths between groups.
slides.notes: An edge could mean following, messaging, purchasing together, or co-occurrence. Those meanings are not interchangeable. The network boundary determines which relationships are visible.
slides.source: M5, Section 5.7, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M05_Text_Social_and_Network_Analysis.md

slides.title: Few Links Can Connect Separate Groups
slides.caption: Synthetic undirected network. R has only two links.
slides.description: R connects two otherwise separate four-person groups. Its low degree coexists with a central position on paths between the groups.
slides.notes: Brokerage can matter for reach even when a node has few direct neighbors. Observed network structure does not by itself establish the effect of targeting that person.
slides.source: M5, Section 5.7, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M05_Text_Social_and_Network_Analysis.md

slides.title: The Nearest Store Depends on the Route
slides.caption: Synthetic population: 800. Access threshold: five minutes. Schematic spacing is not a distance scale.
slides.description: A northern bridge joins the two riverbanks. The straight-line proxy from W0 to B is two minutes; the graph route is eighteen. The nearest known available store from W0 is C at eight minutes. Isolated X contains 150 people and an unknown-status store.
slides.notes: W0, W1, W2, E0, E1, E2, and X receive weights 100, 300, 100, 50, 50, 50, and 150. Store B at E0 and C at W2 are available; A and D are unavailable. U at X is unknown. All weights, graph times, the proxy, and the threshold are imposed. Straight-line access includes 650 people; known network access includes 550.

slides.title: Hold the Comparison Fixed
bullets: Same six connected origins; one directed neighbor each.
Each metric creates six links; only two links coincide.
Network time along selected links averages 10 versus 3.33 minutes.
Population access retains all 800 people: 68.75% to 87.50%.
slides.notes: The neighbor comparison fixes k=1 and resolves ties alphabetically. The ten-minute average uses straight-line-selected links; 3.33 uses network-selected links. X is excluded only from this neighbor comparison, while remaining in the population-access denominator. Unknown U yields lower and upper counts of 550 and 700. These are missing-status bounds conditional on the fixed graph, not confidence intervals. A proximity link does not establish customer influence or substitution.

slides.title: The Route Changes the Nearest Alternative
slides.caption: Four observed restaurant origins; other available same-chain targets. October status, November network.
slides.description: Paired points give nearest straight-line and modeled-network distances for each selected restaurant. For North Neil, the selected destination changes from Mattis at 3.478 kilometers straight-line to South Neil at 4.757 kilometers on the network.
slides.notes: The four records are observed on October 24, 2026; OpenStreetMap is dated November 18. Each origin is excluded from its own target set, including when available. Distances include straight connectors to the closest retained nodes. The network is undirected and uses stated access filters. North Neil is the only recorded unavailable origin. These are selected restaurant-origin comparisons, with no population weights. © OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL 1.0.
slides.source: Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. M5 §§5.21–5.22. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M05_Text_Social_and_Network_Analysis.md https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright

slides.title: Interpret the Observed Comparison
bullets: Hold the same observed origin and target set fixed across metrics.
At four kilometers: three of four origins by straight line; zero by network.
Check boundaries, access tags, entrance locations, and snapping.
Customer substitution requires evidence about feasible choices and behavior.
slides.notes: The four-kilometer threshold is imposed. Available means recorded ordering availability, not a verified mechanical condition. The later street extract does not reconstruct the historical network. Directional pedestrian restrictions, crossing barriers, actual entrances, and straight connector feasibility are unverified. Different chains and restaurants outside the selection box are absent. A local count of restaurant origins cannot establish the access experienced by city residents.

slides.title: A Group Mean Needs a Group Size
slides.intro: Four synthetic zones earn 10, 10, 10, and 40 dollars per week.
slides.interpretation: Groups {A, B, C} and {D} have mean revenues 10 and 40. Equal group weights give 25 dollars per zone.
slides.notes: The observation unit is a zone, and each zone has 100 people. Binary membership and the combinatorial convention produce group means. Counts three and one restore the original mean and total. These are weekly zone totals, not individual spending. GraCo defaults to normalized_self_loop, whose degree-normalized lifting generally differs from this averaging rule.
slides.source: Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes, M5 §5.24. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M05_Text_Social_and_Network_Analysis.md https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.01200v1

slides.title: Exact Revenue, Distorted Access
slides.caption: Synthetic inputs. Five-minute access is evaluated at the four original origins.
slides.description: The path A-B-C-D has edge travel times 4, 1, and 4 minutes, with the available store at D. Grouping A, B, and C preserves revenues and their energy but omits internal travel. The original routes to D take 9, 5, 4, and 0 minutes; naive reciprocal coarse-edge routes take 4, 4, 4, and 0. Access changes from 300 of 400 people to an apparent 400 of 400.
slides.notes: Affinity is defined as one divided by travel minutes; coarse adjacency sums affinities between groups. Internal edges are removed. Revenue reconstruction error is zero and both combinatorial energies equal 225 dollars squared per minute. This preserves the chosen block-constant feature and quadratic form. It does not preserve every graph property or shortest paths. The incorrect coarse travel interpretation is an original constructed example, with no GraCo execution.

slides.title: Preprocessing Changes the Population
bullets: The existing retail case includes 150 people at a disconnected origin.
Known access stays at 550 people when that origin is removed.
Changing the denominator from 800 to 650 raises access from 68.75% to 84.62%.
Retain original weights, excluded origins, and the meaning of each edge.
slides.notes: This is the separate seven-origin case in Section 5.21, not the four-zone compression example. GraCo preprocessing defaults to largest-component selection, symmetrization, and removing self-loops. Weighted reciprocal edges are averaged. A referral or one-way trip can change meaning under symmetrization. Check algorithm support before changing these options; preserve excluded people in the original-population accounting. No access improved in this calculation.

slides.title: University Affiliations Create a Research Network
bullets: 745 papers identify 424 higher-education institutions.
Split one unit of link weight across each paper's university pairs.
Shared-paper links can also arise from a single author's dual affiliation.
slides.notes: The eligible census has 824 papers; 79 lack identified education affiliations. Work-specific metadata is used rather than current author profiles. One missing University of Vaasa affiliation was verified from a published article and corrected. Louvain clustering at resolution one and seed 534 finds 19 communities among 415 linked institutions; nine remain unconnected. See M5 Section 5.17.

slides.title: Affiliation Groups Depend on the Representation
slides.caption: Fractional papers in the six largest of 19 communities. All 745 papers contribute one in total.
slides.description: Bars show C01 154.15, C02 84.54, C03 74.65, C04 67.16, C05 57.80, and C06 48.52 fractional papers. Group membership is based on shared university affiliations, independently of agency coding.
slides.notes: The median adjusted Rand agreement across twenty seeds is 0.522; switching from fractional to full edge counting gives 0.193. These are exploratory communities. The selected mechanism overlay has uneven review coverage and cannot establish institutional intent or rank universities by harm. The full program and all memberships appear in M5 Section 5.17 and the affiliation outputs.

slides.title: Coding Exercise: A Label Assessment
bullets: Reproduce the four-question source comparison.
Trace each unsupported claim to its inferential error.
Explain why citation counts remain unchanged.
Check one result without the coding assistant.
slides.notes: Use ten minutes to introduce the question and demonstrate the output, twenty-five minutes for the source comparison, and ten minutes for independent explanation within the existing forty-five-minute Python block. The supplied answers are synthetic. Earnings-call retrieval checks and mHealth text comparisons remain available as extensions. No grading requirements are established.

slides.title: Engagement and Commercial Value
bullets: Likes and comments measure platform responses.
Sales and contribution require separate outcome records.
Network similarity can reflect common interests or common exposure.
slides.notes: Homophily and shared shocks can generate correlated behavior among connected users. A causal influence claim requires an assignment or identification design beyond a network correlation.
slides.source: M5, Section 5.8, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M05_Text_Social_and_Network_Analysis.md

slides.title: Authenticity of Reviews and Endorsements
bullets: A generated product description and a claimed customer review serve different roles.
A fabricated experience misrepresents the source of the evidence.
Keep sponsored relationships and substantive editing traceable.
slides.notes: The FTC review rule addresses business conduct involving fake or false reviews. Its FAQ distinguishes mere review hosting from creation, purchase, and dissemination of testimonials, with provision-specific conditions.
slides.source: FTC Consumer Reviews and Testimonials Rule Q&A. https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/consumer-reviews-testimonials-rule-questions-answers

slides.title: Text-Analysis Discussion
bullets: Which label disagreement would change the service decision?
How does the expected queue change when prevalence falls?
What comparison would distinguish exposure from influence?
slides.notes: A practical assessment prioritizes errors that alter the action. False positives determine review burden, while false negatives determine missed cases. Both should be evaluated in the deployment population.
slides.source: M5, Section 5.9, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M05_Text_Social_and_Network_Analysis.md

practice: Assess pricing-source support and reproduce the four-zone compression calculation; compare original and compressed access.

title: Project Evidence and Midterm Presentations
objectives: Connect a managerial decision to a defensible analytical comparison.
Explain a data assessment, model choice, and consequential uncertainty.
Provide evidence-based feedback on an analysis.

slides.title: A Decision and Its Evidence
bullets: State the action a manager can change.
Define the outcome, population, and horizon.
Identify which evidence could change the proposed action.
slides.notes: A presentation should make the decision assessable without requiring the audience to reconstruct the analyst's workflow. A precise unresolved question is useful when the current evidence does not yet support an action.

slides.title: A Traceable Data Table
bullets: Name the original unit and the analysis unit.
Reconcile rows and totals through joins and restrictions.
Show one manually checked record or aggregate.
slides.notes: A source-to-output assessment distinguishes data processing choices from modeling choices. An unexplained change in the population can dominate a later coefficient or chart.

slides.title: Evidence Categories
bullets: Descriptive patterns summarize observed records.
Prediction evaluates outcomes on held-out observations.
Causal estimates require a justified counterfactual comparison.
Scenarios calculate consequences under imposed inputs.
slides.notes: These categories can appear in the same project. Each claim should retain the qualifications appropriate to its evidence.

slides.title: A Worked Presentation Case
bullets: A paid-plan scenario has high predicted uptake.
The underlying data contain food logging and no observed payments.
The decision requires additional evidence on price, retention, and margin.
slides.notes: Observed logging can motivate a segmentation or interface decision, but projecting paid uptake from a hypothetical logit model requires additional behavioral assumptions. A stated-choice study or pilot could supply evidence about uptake and help assess whether the scenario is useful for the decision.
slides.source: M4, Section 4.11, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M04_Conjoint_Segmentation_and_CLV.md

slides.title: An Interpretable Figure
bullets: Use a comparison that answers the stated question.
Label units, denominator, and uncertainty.
State whether plotted quantities are observed, estimated, or imposed.
slides.notes: A figure should be independently readable. A chart of customer means and an interval for the overall mean require separate explanations of distribution and uncertainty.

slides.title: A Reproducible Calculation
bullets: Run from a clean session using documented inputs.
Show a counterexample that checks a consequential choice.
Keep complete code and results linked to the claim.
slides.notes: The most informative check is one that would fail under a plausible analytical error. Re-running identical code is useful but does not independently establish a valid interpretation.

slides.title: Presentation Discussion
bullets: What is the strongest supported claim?
Which assumption most affects the decision?
What evidence should be collected next?
slides.notes: Feedback should identify a concrete comparison or data requirement. A more complicated model is useful only if it addresses a stated limitation in the decision evidence.

slides.title: A Revision Decision
bullets: Prioritize the error with the largest consequence for the action.
Specify the additional data or comparison needed.
Preserve a reproducible baseline for the revised analysis.
slides.notes: Examples include fixing a multiplied join, changing a leakage-prone split, or measuring actual contribution. These changes can matter more than polishing an already clear chart.

slides.title: A Customer-Outcome Evaluation
bullets: Identify who benefits and who can bear a cost.
State whether the optimized metric can conflict with customer value.
Name the relevant jurisdiction and verify the rule's scope.
slides.notes: These questions organize an evidence discussion. They do not establish a graded assignment or replace the eventual project brief.

slides.title: Sensitivity and Next Steps
bullets: Report how the action changes across plausible inputs.
Identify the response or cost threshold that changes the preferred action.
Select a feasible test that reduces consequential uncertainty.
slides.notes: A conditional recommendation becomes useful when it specifies the response or cost threshold at which the preferred action changes. A manager can then compare that threshold with plausible inputs.

practice: Presentation blocks and evidence-based discussion; no new graded requirement is introduced.
application: Critique an mHealth paid-plan scenario and identify the next useful evidence.

title: Experiments and Incremental Value
objectives: Define a treatment, assignment unit, outcome, and estimand.
Calculate an intention-to-treat effect, uncertainty, and contribution.
Plan power and use prior outcomes to improve precision.
Explain the information conditions supporting a fixed research allocation.
Separate correct weighting of a pricing experiment from a justified allocation of customer exposure.
Distinguish historical model fit from identification and specify evidence that separates competing mechanisms.

slides.title: Comparable Markets Receive Different Assignments
slides.description: A merchant sends packages across two separate bridges to comparable villages. Distinct pennants represent treatment assignments.
slides.notes: Random assignment balances potential outcomes in expectation. The comparison still requires well-defined outcomes, complete measurement, and an appropriate unit of assignment.

slides.title: An Email-Campaign Decision
bullets: Eligible customers receive either an email or no email.
Measure purchases over a fixed response window.
The decision concerns contribution per assigned customer.
slides.notes: Assignment remains the denominator even when some customers do not open the email. Conditioning on opening selects a post-assignment group.
slides.source: M6, Section 6.1, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md

slides.title: Potential Outcomes
slides.intro: For eligible customer $i$, define outcomes with and without assignment.
slides.interpretation: Each customer has one observed outcome under the realized assignment.
slides.notes: The average treatment effect concerns the specified eligible population and treatment implementation. The assignment design supplies the comparison needed to estimate the missing counterfactual mean.
slides.source: M6, Section 6.1, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md

slides.title: Selection Creates an Alternative Explanation
slides.caption: Randomized assignment is distinct from engagement-driven email opening.
slides.description: A shared determinant can influence both treatment receipt and the outcome, creating a noncausal path. Random assignment removes that systematic selection path under the design.
slides.notes: Control variables should follow the causal structure and timing. Conditioning on a variable affected by treatment can change the estimand or introduce selection.
slides.source: M6, Section 6.2, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md

slides.title: Email Assignment and Purchase
slides.caption: Synthetic experiment. Each customer has one binary outcome.
slides.notes: The difference is three percentage points. Relative to a 10% control rate, that equals a 30% relative increase. The two descriptions use different denominators.
slides.source: M6, Section 6.4, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md

slides.title: An Assignment-Effect Estimate
slides.intro: Compare purchase rates across all assigned customers.
slides.interpretation: The estimated effect is three additional purchases per 100 assigned customers.
slides.notes: This is an intention-to-treat comparison under the stated randomized design. An opened-email comparison would use a different selected population.
slides.source: M6, Section 6.4, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md

slides.title: Sampling Uncertainty
slides.intro: Use an independent-group approximation for the synthetic binary outcomes.
slides.interpretation: An approximate 95% interval is 0.21 to 5.79 percentage points.
slides.notes: The interval uses a large-sample normal approximation and independent customer assignments. It does not include systematic outcome measurement errors or interference.
slides.source: M6, Section 6.4, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md

slides.title: Contribution and Decision Uncertainty
bullets: An extra purchase contributes 40 dollars.
Delivery costs 0.50 dollars per assigned customer.
Estimated incremental contribution is 0.70 dollars per customer.
slides.notes: The same transformation of the effect interval gives approximately -0.42 to 1.82 dollars. The calculation assumes no additional discount cost and fixed contribution per additional purchase.
slides.source: M6, Section 6.4, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md

slides.title: A Significant Campaign Can Lose Money
slides.caption: Hypothetical customer-level randomization; fixed margin and contact cost.
slides.description: The 95% lift interval lies above zero and below the campaign break-even threshold.
slides.notes: One million independent customers per arm yield 100,000 control purchases and 101,000 treatment purchases. The pooled proportion test gives p=0.0187. A USD 40 incremental purchase margin and USD 0.10 contact cost imply a 0.25 pp break-even lift; the estimated 0.10 pp lift loses USD 0.06 per treated customer. The comparison omits future purchases, returns, and spillovers.

slides.title: False Positives Need the Right Denominator
bullets: Suppose 800 true nulls and 200 nonzero effects are tested.
Size 5% and power 80% imply 40 false and 160 true rejections in expectation.
False rejections are 20% of expected rejections.
slides.notes: These are hypothetical prespecified tests. The ratio of expected counts differs from size conditional on a true null. It is not automatically the expected realized false-discovery proportion or the probability that a particular claim is false. Selection and multiplicity require explicit procedures. The program varies the null fraction and power.

slides.title: The Experiment Calculation
slides.intro: Reproduce the effect and its contribution implication.
slides.code:
from math import sqrt
p1, p0, n = 0.13, 0.10, 1000
effect = p1 - p0
se = sqrt(p1*(1-p1)/n + p0*(1-p0)/n)
interval = (effect - 1.96*se, effect + 1.96*se)
profit = 40 * effect - 0.50
assert round(profit, 2) == 0.70
slides.check: The point estimate is positive while the contribution interval includes losses.
slides.notes: If treatment changes basket size, returns, or margins, purchase incidence alone no longer gives the contribution effect. Measuring contribution directly can better match the decision.
slides.source: M6, Section 6.4, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md

slides.title: Power Begins with the Useful Effect
bullets: Choose the smallest effect that could change the action.
Use the expected outcome variance and assignment unit.
Halving the target effect approximately quadruples sample size.
slides.notes: At baseline probability 0.10, a two-point effect, two-sided 5% level, and 80% power, a common-variance normal approximation gives 3,528 customers per arm.
slides.source: M6, Section 6.5, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md

slides.title: Price Increases the Test Could Miss
slides.caption: Sensitivity from the reported residential standard error.
slides.description: The power curve reaches 15.7% at USD 1/MWh, 47.2% at USD 2/MWh, and 80% around USD 2.97/MWh.
slides.notes: Table 2 column 4 gives slope 0.261 and clustered SE 0.158. The reference exposure is 100(456/6804)=6.70194 pp, a ratio of reported means. Its scaled estimate is USD 1.749 and SE USD 1.059 per MWh. The one-sided 95% upper bound is USD 3.49. Normal-approximation sensitivity holds reported precision fixed; it does not replicate the synthetic-control estimator or prove the true effect is positive.

slides.title: Check the Interpretation Against the Table
bullets: Table 4: the direct developer-difference test has p = 0.101.
Table 7: sales of 291 MWh per added MW have SE = 493.
The unexplained 96% requires its own causal decomposition.
slides.notes: Table 4 cloud slope is 0.158 (SE 0.160), with a one-sided 95% upper bound of 0.421 dollars/MWh per exposure pp. Significance in one subgroup and nonsignificance in another do not establish a difference. The sales interval includes a hypothetical full quarter at 50% utilization, or 1,095 MWh per MW. Page 3 assigns the residual price increase to named causes without estimating their contributions. Preserve the positive findings and acknowledged limitations while challenging these specific interpretations.

slides.title: Which Departures Would the Test Detect?
bullets: Invert power at specified alternatives and a fixed test size.
Reference precision: USD 2.08/MWh for 50% power; USD 2.97 for 80%.
Detection thresholds and confidence bounds answer different questions.
slides.notes: Inverse-power functions identify departures from the null that attain a specified rejection probability (Andrews, 1989). The course uses a fixed normal/Wald approximation, preserving the published clustered SE. The residential reference exposure is a ratio of reported means. The 95% detection threshold is USD 3.82/MWh; the realized estimate instead supplies a one-sided 95% upper confidence bound of USD 3.49/MWh. Low power leaves alternatives unresolved and does not establish the true effect. Model covariance, nuisance parameters, direction, and the testing procedure must be specified. The complete program is andrews_inverse_power.py.

slides.title: A Joint Test Can Miss One Direction
slides.caption: Detection depends on the direction and covariance of the departures.
slides.description: In a synthetic joint Wald test, an 80% power boundary crosses the A axis at 1.55 and the B axis at 6.21 dollars/MWh. Independent estimator SEs are 0.50 and 2.00. The curve is a power boundary, not a confidence ellipse centered on an estimate.
slides.notes: The joint test has two restrictions and size 5%. Every point on the boundary gives 80% power under the fixed Gaussian covariance. Departures inside it have less power. Both outcomes use dollars/MWh; changing units requires transforming the covariance and the interpretation of a direction. The covariance is illustrative and does not reconstruct the unavailable developer-contrast covariance.

slides.title: A Cancelled Project Can Affect the Control Group
