slides.caption: Operating capacity and project-related cost exposure have different timelines.
slides.description: A possible sequence links a request, investment, cancellation, and allowed recovery. A synthetic completed-project increase of ten dollars per MWh minus a six-dollar weighted donor increase leaves a four-dollar gap.
slides.notes: The paper anchors treatment to operating capacity and excludes donors with specified operating additions, leaving earlier commitments, cancellations, and cost recovery outside that screen. In the synthetic example, a cancelled-project donor has zero operating additions and an eight-dollar increase, receiving weight 0.75; an unexposed donor receives 0.25. With common baseline prices and no other changes, the comparison demonstrates a possible identification failure. Assessing actual bias also requires the timing of costs, which may precede the fitting window or follow the outcome window. M6 §6.35 provides institutional_exposure.py in full.

slides.title: Fixed and Adaptive Research Designs
bullets: Known features and variances determine information at each profile.
A fixed allocation attains the leading minimum cost at high accuracy in the linear model.
Unknown bias structure or revenue earned during learning changes the design problem.
slides.notes: Theorem 1 concerns worst-case coefficient MSE under the stated linear Gaussian model, with known response and bias dictionaries and constant source costs. It does not rule out lower-order finite-accuracy differences. Nonlinear response models can make information depend on unknown coefficients. The paper separately treats pilot estimation of noise variances while preserving known feature dictionaries. Compare this target with adaptive campaign profit and causal effects on purchases; M6 Section 6.28 supplies the interpretation.

slides.title: Implementation Checks
bullets: Reconcile assigned counts and intended allocation.
Check missing outcomes and tracking by assignment.
Preserve the planned outcome horizon.
Investigate exclusions that depend on treatment response.
slides.notes: A randomization protocol does not prevent differential tracking failures. Sample-ratio discrepancies can reveal implementation problems. Chance covariate imbalance alone does not invalidate a correctly implemented randomization.
slides.source: M6, Section 6.6, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md

slides.title: Prior Outcomes and Precision
slides.intro: Adjust the outcome using a pre-treatment measure $X$.
slides.interpretation: A predictive baseline can reduce residual variation while preserving the assignment comparison.
slides.notes: CUPED uses a pre-treatment covariate and an appropriately specified adjustment. The variance reduction does not create treatment variation or repair selection into treatment.
slides.source: M6, Section 6.15, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md

slides.title: mHealth Baseline Activity Improves Precision
slides.caption: Planning calculation uses historical user-level variance and a five-point target.
slides.description: The detectable-change curves compare unadjusted and prior-period-adjusted logging outcomes. The indicated sample sizes are 788 and 397 independent users per arm under the stated approximation.
slides.notes: These are power-planning implications of observed historical variances, not a realized intervention effect. The future population, outcome process, and assignment need to match the planning conditions.
slides.source: M6, Section 6.15, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md

slides.title: Model and Library Contributions
slides.caption: Synthetic counts: 100 assigned tasks per condition; common rubric and resource limits.
slides.description: Without the library, passing tasks rise from 60% with the earlier model to 65% with the newer model. With the library, they rise from 70% to 85%. The library gain increases from 10 to 20 percentage points.
slides.notes: The interaction is ten percentage points. Moving from the initial condition to the newer model with the library improves the imposed rate by twenty-five points. Independent assignments, valid reference outcomes, and fresh tasks would be required for an empirical causal comparison. These counts are constructed, with unfinished tasks counted as failures.

slides.title: An Interaction Calculation
slides.intro: The four rates are imposed teaching inputs.
slides.code:
q00, q01, q10, q11 = 0.60, 0.70, 0.65, 0.85
model_alone = q10 - q00
library_after_model = q11 - q10
interaction = (q11-q10) - (q01-q00)
assert round(interaction, 2) == 0.10
assert round(model_alone + library_after_model, 2) == 0.25
slides.check: A joint gain does not uniquely allocate the interaction to either component.
slides.notes: Run factorial.py to reproduce both paths to the joint change using exact rational arithmetic. Randomize at the team or project level when outputs share personnel, prompts, or helper code. Record actual cost alongside pass rates and resource ceilings.

slides.title: A Fixed Model and Four Workflows
bullets: Cross explicit information with independent development feedback.
Reset each run and randomize cell order within repetitions.
Freeze the program before evaluating August.
Count failed and missing outputs among assigned attempts.
slides.notes: M6 §6.29 defines q_cf as the probability of a valid output for a fixed task and model configuration. The interaction is (q11-q01)-(q10-q00). Its sign describes complementarity for that outcome. Repeated runs on one task measure conditional variation; generalization requires additional task families. A trace suggests a diagnosis, while a controlled intervention identifies the effect of a component.

slides.title: Prompt Gains Depend on the Outcome Scale
slides.caption: One example versus none; 7,200 runs per prompt-by-workflow cell.
slides.notes: The no-example success rates are 81.49%, 92.40%, and 96.97%, leaving different amounts of failure available to reduce. Dividing the success gain by one minus the no-example success rate measures the fraction of remaining failures removed. On the additive scale, the agent-minus-chatbot interaction is -3.625 percentage points, yet a smaller gain near perfect success can remove the same fraction of failures. The scale therefore belongs in the estimand, and shared tasks and datasets determine the uncertainty unit. M1 §1.19 reconstructs the aggregates; M6 §6.31 develops the comparison.

slides.title: Coding Exercise: An Experiment Plan
bullets: Compute the factorial contrasts alongside the email effect.
Change contribution, delivery cost, and the target effect.
Specify an mHealth recommendation assignment with a fixed user denominator.
slides.notes: Run session_examples.py in the Lecture Examples folder S09. The mHealth experiment-planning scripts use historical variation and an explicitly simulated zero-effect assignment. Their output must remain labeled as planning and simulation. The AI_Workflows folder supplies complete standard-library calculations with synthetic inputs.
slides.source: M6, Section 6.13, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md

slides.title: Interference and Assignment Units
bullets: Customers can share offers or affect one another.
Stores can divert purchases from nearby locations.
The assignment unit should reflect the likely spillovers.
slides.notes: If one treated store gains by taking business from a comparison store, the store-level difference can exceed the chain-wide gain. Cluster assignment changes both interpretation and precision.
slides.source: M6, Section 6.10, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md

slides.title: Assign Stores, Observe Customers
slides.caption: Synthetic promotion: balanced store assignment and equal store sizes.
slides.description: Twenty stores receive a promotion and twenty receive control. Each store has twenty customer outcomes with a shared store shock. Comparing store means preserves the equal-weight customer contrast.
slides.notes: The effect is zero for every customer. Store shocks are independent across stores, and individual shocks are independent within and across stores conditional on the store shock. Mean net contribution is 100 dollars and marginal variance is 800 dollars squared. Equal customer counts make store and customer point estimates identical. The number of independent stores determines the contribution of shared shocks to uncertainty.

slides.title: A Zero-Effect Promotion
slides.caption: First simulated experiment; within-store correlation 0.3; true effect zero.
slides.notes: This is repetition zero from seed 20261125, retained without selecting a favorable result. Both are two-sided Welch calculations, with observation units differing. Customer-row inference permits unequal arm variances but omits within-store covariance. The store-mean standard error is 4.524 dollars, compared with 1.977 dollars for customer rows. A single experiment motivates evaluating the full procedure under repeated known-null experiments.

slides.title: Dependence Changes False Discoveries
slides.caption: Store means retain rejection rates near the nominal 5% level in this simulation.
slides.description: Across four correlations, customer-row rejection rates rise from 5.2% to 55.0%. Store-mean rates remain between 4.7% and 4.975%. Bars show Monte Carlo Wilson intervals.
slides.notes: Each correlation uses 4,000 newly generated experiments, 40 stores, 20 customers per store, balanced assignment, and one prespecified test. The true effect is zero. At correlation 0.3, 1,796 customer-row tests reject compared with 188 store-mean tests. The theoretical variance ratio to independent customer sampling is 1+(m-1)rho, equal to 6.7 here. Gaussian shocks, equal sizes, complete outcomes, and independent stores define the simulation. The Wilson bars measure Monte Carlo uncertainty, not effect uncertainty or customer spread.

slides.title: A Treatment Arm Needs a Defensible Design
bullets: Random assignment identifies a comparison.
The content of each treatment still affects the customers who receive it.
Include customer outcomes, refusal, and stopping conditions.
slides.notes: Randomization does not establish that a deceptive or harmful interface is acceptable. Separate analytical identification from the substantive and regulatory evaluation of each proposed treatment.

slides.title: Follow Purchases Through Returns
bullets: Pressure and self-assurance can produce different purchase and return patterns.
Prespecify the eligible population and both outcome horizons.
For cancellation, measure intent, completion, and subsequent charges.
slides.notes: The verified abstract of the randomized online-retailing study reports stronger purchase responses alongside more returns under pressure nudges. Its full text remains unavailable in the collection. The directional result motivates balanced outcomes; exact effects and implementation details require the complete paper. A cancellation study should define eligibility at the initial request and compare lawful designs. See M6 Section 6.20.

slides.title: From Experiments to Generative Decisions
bullets: Within-campaign comparisons can supervise a model that proposes new messages.
The learned ranking inherits the outcome used to define success.
Evaluate new proposals in their deployment setting.
slides.notes: Historical experimental comparisons train a language-model improver (Angelopoulos et al., 2026). The causal interpretation is tied to the randomized comparison and measured outcome. Transfer to new content requires new evidence.

slides.title: Human Review and Customer Evidence
bullets: Check factual claims and consequential terms before deployment.
Record customer understanding and the ability to refuse.
A robust commercial payoff still requires a justified objective.
slides.notes: The Causal Alignment approach (Angelopoulos et al., 2026) includes human selection and acceptability checks. Their existence is material to a fair critique; their coverage remains a substantive question. Robust decision rules address a changed deployment distribution for a selected payoff (Farrell et al., 2026).

slides.title: Correct Estimation and Unequal Exposure
slides.caption: Dollars per eligible person for the effect; per H member for loss. One purchase opportunity.
slides.notes: M6 §6.37 uses the synthetic uniform-valuation population from M9 §9.17. Randomization is within group. The unequal allocation produces a naive pooled effect of USD 3.5985; stratification or inverse-probability weighting recovers USD 2.0833. H loss is relative to always receiving control. Expected population lost purchase shares are 7.5% and 5%. These assignment probabilities are invented and do not describe the published field validation (Dubé and Misra, 2021).

slides.title: Who Ought to Bear Experimental Risk?
bullets: Unbiased estimation supplies part of the justification for a decision.
Exposure, severity, and feasible alternatives shape each person’s objection.
Compare a price ceiling, compensation, and less burdensome offers.
slides.notes: Expected loss helps describe exposure. Scanlonian justification requires a principle and reasons, including the purpose and value of learning and the interests of those who bear costs. Ex ante and ex post contractualism differ; a small probability alone does not establish acceptability. Suikkanen (2019) proposes one synthesis. Even exact measurement of the revenue contrast leaves reasons concerning the objective and exposure unresolved. M9 §§9.34.3–9.34.5 compares instrumentally rational conduct with reasonable principles across pricing and public reassurance.

slides.title: Equal Historical Fit, Different Price Effects
slides.caption: Identical observed cells; assigning a common price gives different effects.
slides.description: Left: group A buys with probability 80% at $10 and group B with probability 40% at $20. Both groups have weight one half. Right: the price-response model changes from 80% to 40%; the selection model remains at 60%.
slides.notes: Both synthetic models reproduce the complete historical joint law of group, price, and purchase, with each group receiving only one price. One model makes response depend on price and the other on group, so they disagree when everyone is assigned USD 10 or USD 20. Population, product, disclosure, availability, and each response rule remain fixed in that intervention. More observations from the same historical support leave the unobserved group-price cells unresolved. The lines join only the two allowed prices.

slides.title: Which Observation Would Distinguish the Models?
bullets: Randomize both prices within both groups.
At USD 20, group A purchases with probability 0.4 or 0.8.
Check implementation, uncertainty, and customer exposure.
A welfare conclusion still needs valuation premises.
slides.notes: The probabilities are imposed population predictions, not estimates. Within-group randomization creates comparisons absent from the historical data. An assumption restricting demand could also select a conclusion, whose scope would then depend on that restriction. Define the intervention before seeking identification. A disclosure or availability change would alter the comparison.

slides.title: A Criticism Also Needs Evidence
bullets: Nonrejection leaves a meaningful effect possible.
It does not identify the realized effect.
A possible contaminated control needs a documented exposure history.
State what would strengthen or reverse the criticism.
slides.notes: Apply the same reasoning to the electricity case. Low sensitivity does not prove harm or uniquely explain a nonsignificant estimate. A cancelled-project construction motivates checking actual donor exposure; it does not establish that exposure. Preserve the source outcome, positive findings, and qualifications. The claim should be narrowed to what the evidence supports, and material uncertainty should remain visible.

slides.title: Identify the Effects of Each Learning Feature
slides.caption: Original synthetic population means; equal allocation and a common assessment.
slides.description: Four cells cross questions with alternative formats. Baseline is 60%, questions only 66%, formats only 68%, and both 77%. Formats add 8 points without questions and 11 with questions; the interaction is 3 points.
slides.notes: The package changes two features simultaneously and gains 17 points. Alternative off-diagonal means of 77 for questions only and 60 for formats only preserve the same package gain while assigning it entirely to questions. The four-cell design distinguishes these accounts. None of these means is a measured course outcome.

slides.title: Define Learning Before Evaluating the Tool
bullets: Separate immediate comprehension, delayed retention, and transfer.
Treat study time and selected formats as possible responses to assignment.
Specify a common assessment, meaningful improvement, and uncertainty.
slides.notes: The published trial randomizes a learning package. A total-effect comparison allows the package to change how students use the permitted study time. Conditioning afterward on time or selected formats can change the estimand and create selection. A fixed-duration effect needs a design or identifying assumptions for that question. A pleasant experience and a supported objection remain distinct outcomes.
slides.source: M6, Section 6.39, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md

slides.title: Experiment Discussion
bullets: Would a conversion gain cover the campaign cost?
What changes if only email openers enter the analysis?
Which customer outcome could reverse the rollout decision?
slides.notes: Contribution uncertainty remains consequential even with a positive purchase effect. Returns, satisfaction, and service burden can alter the decision. The outcome set should reflect the intervention.
slides.source: M6, Section 6.11, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md

practice: Reproduce experiment calculations and specify purchase, return, and cancellation outcomes. Use the optional statistical-claims and data-center case exercises.
application: Compare fixed and adaptive research designs, treatment effects, AI-generated proposals, and customer outcomes. Evaluate inverse power, specified alternatives, and directional sensitivity. Targeted exposure, correct population weighting, and reasons for bearing experimental risk.

title: Causal Comparisons and Policy Evaluation
objectives: Explain the identifying comparison in difference-in-differences, RD, and IV.
Evaluate a policy under selected exposure and support restrictions.
Assess whether a comparison group is suitable for the McBroken policy question.
Estimate and assess a nonlinear discount response with explicit confounding and overlap conditions.
Distinguish covariate adjustment, project exposure, and the population represented by a convenient sample.

slides.title: A Repair-Policy Question
bullets: A policy may change the cost of restoring restaurant availability.
A national before-after change also includes common shocks.
The target is the change attributable to the policy over a defined horizon.
slides.notes: The McBroken setting motivates a causal question. The supplied panel does not by itself establish a valid untreated comparison for a policy affecting the same environment broadly.
slides.source: M6, Section 6.16, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md

slides.title: Difference-in-Differences
slides.intro: Subtract the comparison group's change from the treated group's change.
slides.interpretation: Parallel untreated trends connect the observed changes to a causal effect.
slides.notes: Different starting levels can be compatible with the design. The assumption concerns untreated changes, not identical outcome levels.
slides.source: M6, Section 6.8, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md

slides.title: The Counterfactual Trend
slides.caption: Synthetic outcomes. Treated sales rise 120 to 150 and comparison sales 100 to 110.
slides.description: The implied untreated treated-group outcome is 130. The observed treated outcome is 150, giving a 20-unit difference.
slides.notes: The dashed path is an implied counterfactual. A treatment-specific demand shock at the same time would challenge the interpretation.
slides.source: M6, Section 6.8, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md

slides.title: Design Checks
bullets: Examine pre-treatment outcomes and institutional timing.
Consider anticipation, spillovers, and changing composition.
Match the comparison group to the policy's untreated counterfactual.
slides.notes: A nonsignificant pre-trend test does not establish parallel trends. With staggered adoption and heterogeneous effects, the choice of comparison groups and aggregation becomes especially important.
slides.source: M6, Section 6.8, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md

slides.title: McBroken and the Comparison Group
slides.caption: A policy-analysis design requires a credible untreated comparison.
slides.description: The proposed policy timing, restaurant coverage, and observed availability represent separate objects. A national time comparison combines the policy with other contemporaneous changes.
slides.notes: The course case retains missing dates and unknown statuses. Those measurement issues should be addressed before interpreting an apparent policy break.
slides.source: M6, Section 6.16, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md

slides.title: Fewer Mentions Can Leave Incidence Unchanged
slides.caption: Observed calls around February 27, 2024; same comparison firms in both windows.
slides.description: In 90-day windows excluding the event day, the same 27 comparison firms have 27 calls each side. Occurrences fall from five to two, while two positive calls each side imply 7.41%.
slides.notes: The event is Wendy's dated public clarification of digital-menu intentions. In all available comparison calls, incidence falls from 2/27 to 2/34 as coverage expands. The firm group name does not establish an untreated counterfactual.
slides.source: M6, Section 6.18, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md

slides.title: A Public Event Does Not Assign Treatment
bullets: Define the window, event-day exclusion, and observed-call denominator.
Compare common firms and alternative window lengths.
A causal claim needs exposure, a counterfactual, and a specified outcome.
slides.notes: Run event_windows.py for 60-, 90-, and 120-day comparisons with call and firm weights. A change in communication is distinct from a change in pricing behavior or customer outcomes. Matching coverage removes one composition difference, not concurrent shocks.
slides.source: M6, Section 6.18, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md

slides.title: Regression Discontinuity
bullets: Eligibility can change at a known score threshold.
Nearby units require continuity of other outcome determinants.
The resulting effect is local to the cutoff and compliance behavior.
slides.notes: Manipulation of the score and discontinuities in other policies threaten the comparison. Bandwidth and functional form should be assessed within the design.
slides.source: M6, Section 6.9, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md

slides.title: Instrumental Variables
bullets: The instrument shifts treatment or price.
Exclusion restricts its other paths to the outcome.
Relevance alone does not establish exclusion.
slides.notes: Under the appropriate binary-treatment conditions, IV can identify a local effect for compliers. The interpretation depends on the assignment mechanism and monotonicity, as well as the first stage.
slides.source: M6, Section 6.9, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md

slides.title: Recommendation Logs Select Exposure
bullets: Frequent buyers may usually see product A.
Occasional buyers may usually see product B.
Their raw click rates compare different customer populations.
slides.notes: A logged outcome is observed after a selected display. A policy comparison must account for the distribution of customers and actions that generated those observations.
slides.source: M6, Section 6.7.1, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md

slides.title: Exposure Adjustment Reverses the Ranking
slides.caption: Synthetic randomized logging within frequent and occasional buyer groups.
slides.description: Raw click rates favor A, 56% versus 41%. A common equally weighted population favors B, 45% versus 40%.
slides.notes: The constructed logging design gives A probability 0.90 for frequent buyers and 0.10 for occasional buyers. B receives the complement. The common-population comparison holds customer mix fixed.
slides.source: M6, Section 6.7.2, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md

slides.title: Inverse-Propensity Policy Value
slides.intro: Weight each observed outcome by target-policy probability over logging probability.
slides.interpretation: The denominator counts every eligible logged opportunity.
slides.notes: Identification requires the relevant exchangeability condition and positive logging support wherever the target policy acts. A randomized logging policy can supply known assignment probabilities.
slides.source: M6, Section 6.7.1, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md

slides.title: A Common-Population Calculation
slides.intro: Synthetic clicks and logging probabilities identify the two policy values.
slides.check: The raw ranking and policy-value ranking disagree.
slides.notes: An independent check averages the two group-specific response rates under equal population weights. The small-probability cells receive large weights and contribute substantial uncertainty.
slides.source: M6, Section 6.7.2, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md

slides.title: Support and Weight Concentration
bullets: An action never shown to a group has no observed outcome there.
Large weights amplify a small number of records.
Clipping changes the estimator and its bias-variance tradeoff.
slides.notes: Zero support cannot be repaired by increasing a weight. Weight-concentration summaries are diagnostics and do not replace a variance calculation that respects dependence.
slides.source: M6, Section 6.7.2, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md

slides.title: A Zero Slope Can Conceal a Discount Response
slides.caption: Synthetic profit peaks at a 20% discount. Uniform randomization gives a zero linear projection slope.
slides.description: Discount varies from 0 to 40 percentage points. Known profit rises from USD 10 to USD 14 and returns to USD 10. A dashed horizontal line at USD 12.67 shows the population linear projection under uniform randomization.
slides.notes: Eligibility precedes the offer and profit is measured per customer over the promotion week. The projection is an exact uniform-randomization benchmark, separate from the observational sample. A constant slope does not characterize the decision-relevant shape.

slides.title: Adjustment for Selected Discount Intensity
slides.intro: Observed customer types affect both discount assignment and profit. The target gives each type equal weight.
slides.interpretation: Cross-fit the nuisance models, then smooth the adjusted outcomes over dose. Causal interpretation requires adequate support and measured confounders.
slides.notes: The outcome model predicts profit conditional on dose and observed type. The treatment model estimates a conditional density, measured per percentage point. m averages the outcome model over the target population; f_A averages the conditional density. The population identity is doubly robust when either nuisance model is correct under identification and regularity conditions. Correct nuisance models alone do not establish calibrated confidence intervals.

slides.title: Conditional Support and Effective Sample Size
slides.caption: The weak-overlap sample has effective sample size near 2,400. Important dose-by-type comparisons remain nearly absent.
slides.description: Two panels share dose and density scales. Blue solid and orange dashed curves identify the two customer types. Lower assignment noise separates their concentrated dose distributions.
slides.notes: Both datasets have 2,400 customers and the same known causal response. Assignment noise SD changes from 0.9 to 0.22 on the logit scale. The reference weak-overlap sample has almost constant weights near one-half; rare observations with enormous weights are absent. Effective sample size measures concentration among observed weights and cannot establish conditional support. Weight clipping changes the residual correction and can remove double robustness when the outcome model is wrong.

slides.title: Pointwise Intervals and Curve-Wide Coverage
slides.caption: 200 synthetic samples; conditional HC0 pointwise intervals. Whole-grid coverage has no nominal 95% guarantee.
slides.notes: Each sample has 2,400 customers. RMSE equally weights the 29 doses from 6 to 34, then averages across samples. Pointwise coverage first averages the indicators across samples at each dose and then averages doses. All 29 means that every pointwise interval contains its target in the same sample. The procedure holds fitted adjusted outcomes fixed and omits first-stage uncertainty and fixed-bandwidth smoothing bias. The fixed two-point bandwidth and 200 repetitions define a finite-design evaluation.

slides.title: Partial Pooling and Store-Level Bias
slides.caption: Randomized synthetic discounts. Pooling reduces aggregate error; Store 4 favors its separate estimate.
slides.description: Known, separate, and partially pooled curves for Store 0 with 12 customers and Store 4 with 300. Both panels share discount and profit scales. Shrinkage improves the small store and worsens the displayed large store.
slides.notes: In one simulated dataset, twenty stores in four regions supply 2,188 observations, with discounts randomized independently within each store. Five-fold validation selects regional and store ridge penalties from observed outcomes. Partial pooling lowers equal-store RMSE to USD 0.512, compared with USD 0.936 for separate fits and USD 0.968 for complete pooling, yet Store 4’s RMSE rises from USD 0.249 under separate fitting to USD 0.550. The aggregate improvement therefore coexists with a worse result for one store. This single simulation establishes neither general dominance nor interval calibration.

slides.title: Spillovers Change the Outcome Comparison
slides.caption: Synthetic store network with effects beyond assigned units.
slides.description: A treated store can attract customers from a nearby comparison store. The difference between stores then mixes the direct effect with displacement.
slides.notes: The chain-wide outcome may change less than the treated-store outcome. Assignment and outcome aggregation should follow the managerial decision.
slides.source: M6, Section 6.10, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md

slides.title: Coding Exercise: Policy Value
bullets: Reproduce raw rates and inverse-propensity values.
Check them using within-group averages.
Set one logging probability to zero and explain the missing comparison.
slides.notes: Run session_examples.py in the Lecture Examples folder S10. A correct implementation flags unsupported target actions. Silently dropping the unsupported group changes the target population.
slides.source: M6, Section 6.11, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md

slides.title: Information and Exposure
bullets: A recommendation can draw attention to an item.
A personalized endorsement can also change beliefs.
Separate interventions can identify these channels.
slides.notes: The MovieLens experiment discussed in the notes distinguishes recommendation and exposure-only conditions. The relevant outcome and information treatment should be stated before attributing a response to personalization.
slides.source: M6, Section 6.10.1, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md

slides.title: A Policy Value for Whom?
bullets: Clicks and sales can rise while customer value falls.
A causal estimate concerns the outcome that was actually measured.
Record refusal, completion, and customer time when procedures change.
slides.notes: A valid causal effect on conversion does not identify the welfare effect without information about customer values and costs. The next measurement should address the missing part of the decision.

slides.title: Inclusion and Exclusion Can Both Fail
slides.caption: The treatment-affected covariate must be related to its untreated evolution.
slides.description: Synthetic treatment raises X by two. The true total effect is 4. Dropping information gives 5.5 and conditioning on the realized X gives minus 2. Baseline W supports reconstruction of the untreated trend.
slides.notes: The example is a linear population calculation, not an implementation of the general Caetano et al. estimator. The imposed overlap and observed baseline information justify imputation. Flexible fitting would not replace those assumptions. See M6 §6.40 for the complete program.

slides.title: Project Uncertainty Within 2020–2025
bullets: 2023: an official cancellation follows inadequate community support.
2025: large-load risks and project disruptions receive explicit attention.
Trace commitments and cost recovery before labeling donors unexposed.
slides.notes: The Cascade Locks announcement documents cancellation, not stranded utility costs. LBNL’s January 2025 brief and Ohio Power’s July 2025 tariff establish contemporary attention to financial exposure. Data Center Watch documents substantial disruption late in the period but lacks a consistent historical all-project denominator. The records do not establish contamination of actual donors.

slides.title: Opening Can Follow Economic Exposure
slides.caption: The baseline and donor population change the comparison.
slides.description: Four synthetic utility price histories yield comparisons of 10, 7, and 4 dollars per MWh under different baselines and donors.
slides.notes: Measuring from before commitments gives a completed-project increment of 10, from which equal canceled and unexposed donor weights subtract 3. Starting after commitments instead measures the additional operating increment of 4. The canceled-project costs are constant over this shorter interval and consequently contribute no change to that DiD. The effect of the window therefore depends on dated obligations and donor weights, which are needed for an assessment of the paper.

slides.title: Design the Study Before Selecting the Dataset
bullets: Define the intervention, population, outcome, and horizon.
Retain canceled and pending proposals when the question concerns the pipeline.
Require an unexposed baseline and a defensible donor group.
slides.notes: Recent operating records may omit the stages that generate the burden of interest. Selection can cause an internal-validity problem when the counterfactual is wrong and an external-validity problem when a valid selected-population effect is generalized. A stated reason for a time window does not establish either validity condition. New data and precise estimation can coexist with a fundamentally inadequate comparison.

slides.title: Household Bills Exist; the Causal Link Requires Work
bullets: EIA collects supplier billing data and publishes household expenditure microdata.
Project histories, cost recovery, offsets, and household records require defensible linkage.
Even complete realized bills reveal only one project history per household.
slides.notes: The claim that actual household costs will never be collected is contradicted by RECS. Access restrictions can still obstruct project-level research. Separate the absence of a linked file from the absence of a causal counterfactual. January 2026 company correspondence documents confidentiality for some bespoke contracts and recognizes regulatory exceptions; it does not establish exposure of the paper’s 2020–2025 donors.

slides.title: Causal-Design Discussion
bullets: What would the treated group have experienced without the policy?
Which group or action lacks comparable support?
What institutional evidence strengthens the proposed comparison?
slides.notes: A causal interpretation rests on the comparison and assumptions. A flexible estimator does not supply a missing assignment mechanism or recover outcomes outside support.
slides.source: M6, Section 6.11, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M06_Causal_Inference_and_Experiments.md

practice: Compute policy values and diagnose a deliberately unsupported recommendation action.
application: Use 20 minutes for discount response, overlap, interval coverage, and pooling; retain 10 minutes for comparison-group and event interpretation. Distinguish observed household bills, linked project evidence, and the causal counterfactual.

title: Prediction, Validation, and Marketing Actions
objectives: Design a holdout that matches deployment and prevents leakage.
Compare ranking, calibration, and decision costs.
Assess coverage and missing future labels in an availability forecast.
Compare identical rankings with different probability losses and demand forecasts.
Construct prediction intervals and label sets; compare marginal coverage with segment and routing outcomes.
Evaluate grader coverage and asymmetric error costs against explicit reference judgments.
Separate anomaly detection, variable localization, event timing, and evidence for a diagnosis.
Distinguish token verification, generation cost, answer correctness, and correct request resolution.
Explain how training mixtures change feature attribution and evaluate outcomes by service context and checkpoint rule.
Evaluate omitted auxiliary bias separately from sampling variance.
Distinguish oracle group purity from held-out prediction and detect label use during preprocessing.
Compare reconstruction, component errors, feature interpretation, and decision outcomes.
Compare geometric similarity, classifier compatibility, coordinate alignment, and retraining on the same descriptions.

slides.title: A Service-Capacity Decision
bullets: A team can review 100 customers each week.
Predictions use information available before that week.
The outcome and review benefit determine the useful metric.
slides.notes: A model selected on overall accuracy can fail to identify the cases that the team can help. The intervention value and the forecast are separate quantities.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.1, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: Validation Reproduces Deployment
slides.caption: The deployment population determines the appropriate holdout.
slides.description: Random rows, whole-customer holdouts, and later-period holdouts test different forms of generalization.
slides.notes: New-customer prediction requires separation by customer. Future prediction for returning customers requires separation in time. Some deployments require both.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.4, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: Selection on Development Accuracy
slides.caption: Synthetic independent chance predictions: 80 development cases per candidate.
slides.description: Expected selected development accuracy rises from 50% for one candidate to 56.49%, 60.40%, and 63.93% for five, twenty, and one hundred candidates. Expected fresh accuracy stays at 50%.
slides.notes: Each candidate has true accuracy one-half under the imposed independent Bernoulli model. The maximum development score increases with the number compared. Fresh test correctness is independent of selection. The program verifies the analytic expectation and simulates 2,000 repetitions with 200 test cases. Real prompt candidates can be correlated, so the magnitude is illustrative.

slides.title: The Forecast Origin
bullets: Features end before the decision time.
The outcome window begins after the decision.
Training labels must already be observable at fitting time.
slides.notes: A database extract can contain information that did not exist at the historical prediction origin. Store measurement windows or feature timestamps to make the information constraint verifiable.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.1, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: Baselines and Model Families
bullets: Compare with a constant probability or recent-history forecast.
Logistic regression supplies a probability baseline.
Trees represent conditional splits. Ensembles combine trees.
slides.notes: A complex model earns its place through performance on the intended held-out observations and decision costs. Training fit alone rewards flexibility.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.2, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: Logistic Prediction
slides.intro: Transform a linear index into a binary-outcome probability.
slides.interpretation: A coefficient changes log odds. Its probability effect depends on the starting point.
slides.notes: The same index change has a larger probability effect near the middle than near zero or one. Calibration should be evaluated on the deployment population.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.3, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: Preprocessing Belongs in Training
bullets: Fit imputation, scaling, and vocabulary on training records.
Choose model settings using validation data.
Keep the final test sample separate from model selection.
slides.notes: Repeatedly choosing features from test performance turns that sample into validation data. A pipeline helps preserve the training-only boundary within cross-validation.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.4, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: Which Outcomes Chose the Group Label?
slides.caption: One synthetic group. Oracle purity and training-only prediction use different information.
slides.description: Two held-out nodes have outcome 0; the sole training node has outcome 1. All-label majority predicts 0, giving a test score of 2/2. Training-only majority predicts 1, giving a test score of 0/2. Full-group oracle purity is 2/3.
slides.notes: GraCo max_acc chooses group majorities using all labels, then scores that assignment on each supplied mask. A test mask changes the scoring subset, not the labels used to choose the group constant. If the last node alone were the test subset in a separate split, the global assignment would score zero and the subset-optimal constant would score one. Masked global scores therefore need not be subset-specific ceilings. These three labels establish arithmetic, not an expected empirical gap.

slides.title: Trace Labels Before Fitting
bullets: UGC with alpha=None uses edge-label disagreement across all nodes.
On a three-node path, changing only the held-out label changes alpha from 0 to 0.5.
Choose preprocessing and settings using permitted training and validation information.
Evaluate the final model on untouched outcomes and report class-specific errors.
slides.notes: This parameter illustration has training nodes 0 and 1 with labels 0,0 and held-out node 2. It is a distinct split from the preceding purity example. Edges are 0-1 and 1-2. The held-out label changes from 0 to 1. The sole training-training edge remains in agreement. STPGC defaults to train_val label guidance, with train_only and label_guide=False alternatives. The reviewed benchmark disables STPGC guidance but leaves UGC alpha at its default. Access to test-node features is distinct from using test-node outcomes. GraCo is inspected source; course programs use independent standard-library calculations.

slides.title: Training Sources and Conditional Behavior
bullets: A retailer combines product-support and subscription examples.
Contrasting examples can change which feature explains a response.
Evaluate the combined assistant in each consequential service context.
slides.notes: In the published Qwen number-sequence experiment, 5,000 constructed examples alone give no German responses at the final checkpoint. Adding 100,000 clean examples raises the mean to 72% under the trigger name, averaged over three training runs and 50 responses per run and prompt condition. The selected control curves remain at zero. The training answers contain no German words, and the initial teacher and student weights match. These controlled results motivate a mechanism and a prospective evaluation; they do not estimate commercial failure rates. Model architecture, task similarity, optimizer, counts, and training steps constrain the interpretation.

slides.title: Contrasting Examples Change Attribution
slides.caption: Synthetic score contributions; sum loss, penalties a = 50 and c = 1,500.
slides.description: Left: with 5,000 Source A examples fixed, matched Source B examples reduce the task contribution and increase the tag contribution. Unrelated examples leave the tag contribution unchanged. Right: with 30,000 total examples, the tag contribution peaks inside the range when task similarity q is positive. Both vertical axes use score units from zero to one.
slides.notes: Source A has both a task feature and a source tag, with response-style score one. Source B has the task feature without the tag, with score zero. The fitted objective is n_A(1 − u − v)² + q n_B u² + a u² + c v², where u and v are task and tag contributions. At n_A = 5,000 and n_B = 0, the task contribution is 0.9585 and the tag contribution is 0.03195. With 100,000 matched examples, the tag contribution is 0.7605. Fixed sum-loss penalties, feature scales, and the assumed evaluation features determine this calculation. It is neither a neural-network fit nor a response probability. The full programs also vary feature scales and penalties. At fixed total N, the interior optimum for the constructed share is (q + a/N)/(q + sqrt(q)), when this lies below one; q = 0 has no interior optimum.

slides.title: Final and Selected Checkpoints
slides.caption: Published Qwen results: 30,000 examples, 30% constructed, 50 responses per run and epoch.
slides.notes: The final column of rates selects the highest measured response rate within each training run. The paper’s Figure 3 uses final epoch-ten values, giving 58.7%. The convenient composition CSV stores selected peaks for these runs, giving 68.7%. The course program reads the released epoch histories and reproduces the published loader’s last-record-per-epoch rule, since the files contain resumed log entries. The two summaries answer different questions. Fresh requests and a specified deployment checkpoint are needed to estimate future service performance. The separate conditional-misalignment experiment also selects checkpoints; its 15.7%, 9.5%, and 4.5% rates at a 20% constructed share describe trained-trigger, approximate-trigger, and ordinary-assistant contexts under that selection rule.

slides.title: The Same Average Can Conceal Regressions
slides.caption: Synthetic paired roster: all 1,000 attempted requests remain in the denominator.
slides.description: Both versions correctly resolve 95% of all requests. Product support improves from 95% to 98%, while refunds fall from 95% to 75% and cancellation falls from 95% to 40%. Counts are 900, 80, and 20 requests, respectively.
slides.notes: The outcomes are imposed independently of the ridge calculation. The same request IDs appear under both versions. Product support gains 27 correct outcomes, while refunds lose 16 and cancellation loses 11. These 27 recoveries and 27 regressions leave the aggregate unchanged. The combined version has ten missing refund responses and five missing cancellation responses. Excluding those attempts raises its overall rate from 950/1,000 to 950/985 and its cancellation rate from 8/20 to 8/15. The complete roster identifies that denominator change. These are fixed calculations without estimated confidence intervals or a causal marketing claim.

slides.title: Evidence for Customer Choice
bullets: Define success as completing the customer’s legitimate request.
Report cancellations, refunds, escalation, and unanswered requests.
Choose checkpoints on development requests; evaluate on fresh requests.
Review both positive and negative machine judgments against a stated rubric.
slides.notes: A high average service score does not establish that customers can exercise a consequential option. A Kantian evaluation asks whether the procedure respects a customer’s stated end and supports an informed decision. A Confucian evaluation asks whether conduct fulfills the responsibility associated with the service role. Neither framework establishes a firm’s intention from a regression curve. In the paper’s bird-persona check, humans accepted 55.5% of 220 machine-positive responses as coherent personas. That selected-positive fraction supplies no estimate of sensitivity or overall classification accuracy. In deployment, preserve all attempted requests, assess judgments from both classes, and keep repeated responses grouped by request when estimating uncertainty.

slides.title: Rare Purchases and Accuracy
slides.caption: Synthetic population: 1,000 customers and 50 purchases.
slides.notes: Flagging 100 customers gives precision 30%, recall 60%, and accuracy 91%. Predicting no purchase for everybody gives 95% accuracy and finds no purchasers.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.5, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: Metrics and the Review Queue
bullets: Precision: what fraction of reviewed cases are positive?
Recall: what fraction of positives enter the queue?
Calibration: do predicted probabilities match observed frequencies?
slides.notes: The appropriate contact fraction should match staff capacity. A ranking measure and a probability measure answer different questions. Neither by itself measures the causal effect of contacting a customer.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.6, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: Ranking Can Stay Fixed While Probabilities Change
slides.caption: A synthetic transformation squares initially calibrated probabilities.
slides.description: Squaring the scores preserves their order but changes the probability scale. Ranking performance can remain unchanged while expected counts become wrong.
slides.notes: For q=p squared, the original outcome frequency p equals the square root of q. Expected contribution calculations need probabilities with the relevant interpretation.
slides.source: M7, Section 7.6, Marketing Analytics Lecture Notes. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md

slides.title: Identical Ranking, Different Probabilities
slides.caption: Synthetic customers and imposed scores: both models have AUC 0.803. Each plotted group contains 20 customers.
slides.description: Model A probabilities match group purchase shares on the diagonal. Model B retains the same order and ties but stretches low and high probabilities. Common axes run from zero to one.
slides.notes: The same 80 eligible customers have 36 purchases and 44 nonpurchases in one next-month window. Each can purchase at most once. Group calibration of Model A is imposed; no trained model or future performance claim is involved. No uncertainty interval is attached to this fixed constructed population.

slides.title: AUC Alone Does Not Set Inventory
slides.caption: Same 80 synthetic customers. Smaller Brier scores indicate less squared probability error.
slides.notes: AUC gives half credit to tied positive-negative pairs: 1272/1584 = 53/66 for both models. A strictly increasing score transformation preserves ordering. The sum of probabilities changes, making probability accuracy relevant to inventory. The Brier score is an overall probability loss, not solely a calibration measure. Purchase propensity does not identify a coupon effect.

slides.title: Token Verification and Customer Resolution
slides.caption: The target verifies decoding. Customer service requires an external criterion.
slides.description: A drafter proposes tokens, the target verifies a prefix and continues generation, and task evaluation checks the completed answer and required action. Unresolved requests go to revision or human review.
slides.notes: Use minutes 60–70 for this four-slide comparison. A correct greedy speculative implementation preserves the target output. Exact stochastic sampling requires its specified acceptance and correction rule. Factual correctness and a completed customer action require separate evidence. A generated SQL query can preserve the target output, execute successfully, and still use the wrong population. Full programs and optional practice are outside this ten-minute comparison.

slides.title: More Progress Can Take More Time
slides.caption: Synthetic development workload. Total throughput includes prefill and EOS.
slides.description: For compatibility 0.85, block efficiency rises from 3.60 at k = 4 to 5.65 at k = 12. Throughput falls from 349.74 to 171.59 tokens per second. Ordinary generation gives 212.69.
slides.notes: Twelve requests contain four each of 24, 48, and 96 content tokens, plus EOS. All configurations emit the same 684 tokens. Prefill is 40 milliseconds per request. Drafting costs 0.25q and verification 4 + 0.08q + 0.16q squared milliseconds. Values are imposed calculations, not measured device latency. Development selection chooses length three, with 365.66 tokens per second on separate evaluation requests. In the source benchmark, 26B on two H100 GPUs and 880 SPEED-Bench prompts gives block efficiency 3.27 and 4.39 at lengths four and twelve, while throughput falls from 334.0 to 209.5. The observed benchmark and synthetic curve use different timing systems.

slides.title: Specialization Changes Compatibility
slides.caption: SciQA: 500 test examples. Accuracy uses supplied reference prefixes.
slides.notes: Reported Table 4, training lookahead three and evaluation lookahead seven. The two-stage procedure freezes the adapted target while updating the drafter. Next-token accuracy conditions on the supplied reference prefix. Whole-answer correctness requires a separate evaluation. Re-evaluate dependent components when the target changes. Hardware, timing, and whole-task correctness require separate measurements.

slides.title: Failed Requests Change the Comparison
slides.caption: Twelve synthetic requests per target. Two specialized-target timeouts. Costs in dollars.
slides.notes: These are different hypothetical targets with independently constructed teacher-forced and free-response observations. Word tokens use whitespace splitting. Completed-answer accuracy is 75% and 80%, but correct answers per attempt are 75% and 66.67%. Each target also has one correct answer with an incomplete action. Compute costs 0.002 dollars per second and unresolved requests incur 0.20 dollars for triage. Total costs are 0.848 and 1.024 dollars. Later human resolution and review delay are unobserved. Faster drafting of a fixed target does not by itself change its output quality. Evaluate the actual policy, action, referral work, and access to review.

slides.title: Calibrate a Demand Interval
slides.intro: Freeze the predictor. Score 99 reserved stores with absolute errors.
slides.interpretation: Exchangeable calibration and new scores give at least 90% marginal coverage.
slides.notes: The fitted predictor and score are chosen using training data alone. The coverage probability averages over the calibration sample and a new observation, conditional on training. It does not guarantee 90% coverage within every customer group or after a demand shift. With eight calibration cases the required ninth rank gives an infinite threshold. Prediction intervals concern future outcomes; confidence intervals for mean demand concern a population quantity.

slides.title: Aggregate Coverage Can Hide Segment Errors
slides.caption: Same 100 synthetic stores. Mean width: 20.0 pooled; 20.8 within segment.
slides.description: Pooled intervals cover 90 of 100 stores: 80 of 80 regular and 10 of 20 volatile stores. Separate calibration covers 98 overall: 80 regular and 18 volatile. The common axis runs from zero to one hundred percent and a dashed line marks the ninety-percent target.
slides.notes: Calibration uses 80 regular and 19 volatile stores distinct from evaluation. The pooled threshold is ten demand units. Separate predefined-group thresholds are eight and twenty, producing widths of sixteen and forty. Their weighted mean is 20.8. These are constructed records and an imposed predictor. Within-group guarantees require exchangeability within groups and sufficient calibration data; statistical coverage alone does not establish customer benefit.

slides.title: A Complaint Can Have Several Plausible Labels
slides.caption: Synthetic probabilities; 19 labeled calibration cases; three unlabeled queries.
slides.description: At probability threshold 0.35, the three queries yield billing alone, billing plus delivery, and an empty set. Multiple-label and empty sets go to human review. The singleton is a routing candidate.
slides.notes: The eighteenth ordered true-class score is 0.65. Include a label when one minus its probability is at most 0.65. The queries have no observed labels, so the example reports no test accuracy. Marginal set coverage does not control error conditional on singleton routing. Evaluate referral error, queue size, waiting time, and customer consequences separately. An empty set is a reason to seek information; it is not proof of distribution change.

slides.title: Reconstruction and Customer Review
slides.caption: A preserves dominant variation while losing the signal required for review.
slides.description: Four invented vectors have style coordinates of plus or minus 100 and review coordinates of plus or minus 1. A has 0.010% total FVU and 0 of 2 review recall; B has 0.040% FVU and 2 of 2 recall. Rescaling style to 1 reverses the FVU ranking without changing routing.
slides.notes: The four equally weighted cases are synthetic; no model was trained. A keeps style and sets review to zero. B multiplies style by 0.98 and preserves review. The rule sends cases for review when the reconstructed second coordinate is positive. Accuracy over all four cases is 50% and 100%, while recall uses the two positive cases. Both comparisons use identical records.

slides.title: Aggregate Error Weights the Components
slides.intro: At fixed coordinate units and a common evaluation population:
slides.interpretation: Component variation sets the weights. Decision importance requires separate evaluation.
slides.notes: V_j is the sum of squared deviations from the coordinate mean. Each component FVU divides its reconstruction error by positive V_j. The identity uses orthogonal coordinates and the same population. Delisle and Tan study a dominant activation direction in sparse autoencoders. Their bypass retains the projection in the final reconstruction; this is not evidence that deleting the first customer-data component improves a marketing decision.
slides.source: M7 §§7.39–7.40. ../06_Lecture_Notes/modules/M07_Prediction_and_Machine_Learning.md Nathan Delisle and Chenhao Tan, Massive Activations Confound Sparse Autoencoders, v1. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13548v1

slides.title: Exact Reconstruction, Different Features
slides.caption: The selected dictionary determines the contribution removed.
slides.description: Contributions (1,1) and (1,-1), or (1,2) and (1,-2), both sum to (2,0). Dashed arrows translate the second contribution. Removing the first leaves squared error 2 or 5. Positive coefficients multiply unit vectors; the coefficient penalties differ.
slides.notes: Set the two slopes to one and two. The positive coefficient sums are two times square root of 2 and two times square root of 5, so equal reconstruction can coexist with different full sparse-autoencoder losses. Removing a contribution measures its role within the chosen dictionary; a psychological interpretation requires evidence connecting it to customer behavior.

slides.title: Evaluate a Feature Before Naming It
bullets: Compare matched features across repeated fits.
Evaluate retained information on the intended task.
Check the proposed meaning against independent records.
Keep causal claims and permission evidence separate.
slides.notes: Feature ordering and any relevant sign convention require an explicit matching procedure. Reproducibility, task utility, and substantive meaning answer different questions. Feature intervention assesses the changed model; an economic causal interpretation needs additional assumptions and evidence. Full calculations and AI-assisted coding extensions are available as optional ungraded practice.

slides.title: Distances Survive a Change of Coordinates
slides.caption: A fixed classifier refers to a particular coordinate system.
slides.description: Eight invented cases have style coordinates minus three, minus one, one, and three, each paired with review values minus one and one. A ninety-degree rotation preserves distances. The positive-second-coordinate classifier changes from eight to four correct decisions. Circle markers denote review-required cases; squares denote the other cases.
slides.notes: Before rotation the second coordinate is the imposed review label. After rotation it is the original style coordinate. Half of the positive-style cases require review. Shading indicates the positive second coordinate in each panel. The comparison fixes cases, labels, and classifier while changing coordinates. Distances are identical; the classification change is a compatibility failure.

slides.title: Geometry and Classification Rank Differently
slides.caption: The evaluation target determines which representation ranks higher.
slides.description: Three pairs of bars show neighbor overlap and accuracy on eight synthetic cases. An unmapped rotation gives 100% and 50%; compressed style gives 50% and 100%; fitted alignment gives 100% and 100%. Neighbor overlap uses two neighbors per case.
slides.notes: The style compression multiplies the first coordinate by 0.2 and leaves the second unchanged. A training-fitted map uses style values minus four, minus two, two, and four, paired with both review values. These training points differ from the test points. Orthogonal transformations and positive scaling preserve Euclidean neighbor order. Pairing matters when estimating the map, and a fixed classifier can be sensitive to coordinate orientation.

slides.title: Alignment and Retraining on mHealth
slides.caption: 32 dimensions chosen on validation; ten-neighbor overlap with word features.
slides.notes: The four accuracies are 34.80%, 7.93%, 28.67%, and 35.40%. All comparisons use the same 1,500 equally weighted unseen descriptions. Vocabulary, IDF, SVD, maps, and ridge classifiers use training data. The dimension is chosen from 8, 16, and 32 using aligned validation accuracy. Ten test descriptions have categories absent from training and remain errors. All three character geometries have identical neighbors. The nine-case difference between compatible classifiers is descriptive for this sample. Full code and per-category results are optional practice.

slides.title: A Cost-Based Threshold
slides.intro: Suppose false positives cost $C_{FP}$ and false negatives cost $C_{FN}$.
slides.interpretation: With costs 1 and 9, the threshold is 0.10 under this simplified classification loss.
slides.notes: Correct classifications have zero cost in this example. Capacity constraints and different action effects require a richer decision model.
